pages.title: Purser
pages.description: The privately hosted finance back-end, designed for use by your personal AI Agent.

pages.title: API-first design
pages.description: Mostly headless operation through your AI agent, with server-side calculations and an administrative UI.

sections.text: Purser is a privately hosted finance back-end designed for your personal AI agent. It is mostly headless: day-to-day work happens through the agent over MCP or REST. The web UI provides administrative controls and record inspection. Its operations use the public API and require the corresponding scopes; a normal agent token cannot manage tokens or configuration. Purser is an AI enablement engine. It stores records, performs financial calculations and supplies tools and context to an external agent. It is not an AI and requires no AI subscription. Optional model integrations are described below. An agent's present link opens selected records in full detail for a signed-in person, without including those records in the tool response.

sections.heading: Computation server-side, judgment client-side
sections.text: Purser computes financial results; your agent interprets them. Aggregate tools return answers without requiring the agent to retrieve and sum transactions: spending summary, net worth, balance history, forecast balance, list recurring, list unmatched. The agent decides what to ask and how to narrate it; Purser does the arithmetic.

sections.heading: Optional model integrations
sections.text: Purser can call a separately configured model for categorization and transaction review. These integrations are off by default and use the provider, endpoint and credentials you supply. They can use a local or hosted model; any provider charges or subscription belong to that service. The finance engine works with these integrations disabled. See Configuration.

sections.heading: Token budgets
sections.text: Tool responses are budgeted. Aggregate tools return summaries, not row dumps , targeting well under 500 tokens for a typical answer, and no tool forces the caller to do cross-row math. This keeps answers cheap enough to ask freely and small enough to fit an agent's working context.

sections.heading: Three-tier answers
sections.text: Visualization-worthy tools answer in three tiers, so a caller takes exactly what it can use: 1. a one-sentence text headline — enough to narrate; 2. compact structuredContent — a declared, validated shape within the token budget; 3. a meta.ui.resourceUri naming a self-contained widget for MCP Apps hosts. Full-resolution series stay out of the structured payload behind purser:// resources, which share the same auth and are exempt from the budget. The read series tool returns the same series, byte for byte, to clients and gateways that forward tools but not resources — it shares the exemption, so it is read only when the compact answer is not enough. A host with no widget support still gets a complete answer from tiers 1 and 2. Every other tool also carries its answer as text, and an empty list arrives as [], so a gateway that rebuilds results from their text blocks never loses a "nothing found" answer.

sections.heading: Describe first
sections.text: In every fresh session an agent calls describe first. One call returns the data model, amount conventions, the caller's token scopes, the category tree, and the account list. The same guide is served unauthenticated at GET /llms.txt, and the search docs tool answers questions about operating Purser from this documentation.

sections.heading: Why the UI is admin-only
sections.text: The web UI covers setup, connections, settings, tokens and auditing. It also provides account registers, schedules, positions and a forecast chart for direct inspection. Its navigation is Dashboard , Accounts (each opens its register), Scheduled transactions , Import , and one Settings area: General, Connections, Categories, Rules, Agent memory, Prices, Agents & API, Security, Users and Audit log. A member sees the sections their own access works in; the admin-only ones (General, Security, Users, Audit log) are hidden from them. Your agent is the intended interface for day-to-day work. Grafana supplies broader dashboards over the stable read schema. Both use the same underlying financial data and public interfaces. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md sections 1 (principles) and 10 (the MCP toolset and presentation layer).

pages.title: Balances
pages.description: Why a balance is recorded rather than recomputed, the three methods that produce one, and why you should never derive a balance by summing rows.

sections.text: A balance in Purser is recorded, not recomputed . Every surface that shows one — the register's Balance column, the account headline, the REST endpoints, the agent tools — reads a stored number rather than adding up transactions on demand. This page explains what is stored, the three ways a balance is produced, and the one rule that matters if you are an agent.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.text: Never derive a balance by summing rows. Purser already knows the answer, and summing a page of transactions cannot reproduce it: a page is a window, corrections supersede rows rather than editing them, and voided rows still appear in history. Ask for the balance you want instead.

sections.heading: Running balances are stored per row
sections.text: Purser keeps a running balance for every (account, transaction) pair where that transaction has a posting on that account. The number is the account's balance immediately after that transaction, accumulated in a fixed total order so it never depends on how a query happened to sort. That order is (date, created at, transaction id), ascending for accumulation and exactly reversed in the register. The transaction id is the final tiebreak because every row imported in one database transaction can share the same date and creation timestamp. Stored running balances and display order use the same canonical key, so same-day balances stay stable. It is derived data — rebuildable from postings at any time, never authoritative over them — but it is maintained transactionally : the recompute happens inside the same database transaction as the write that invalidated it. A reader can never observe a stale register. A nightly job re-checks the whole store against the postings and rebuilds if anything disagrees. Two consequences worth knowing: - A balance exists only for chain-head rows that are pending or posted. A voided row, a superseded correction, or an expected row has no running balance, and surfaces render it blank rather than repeating the previous row. - The same transaction has a different running balance in each account it touches. A transfer has two. This is why a balance is only meaningful from a named account's perspective.

sections.heading: The three methods
sections.text: What a surface reports as an account's balance depends on the account type, and every response says which method produced it via balance method (method on GET /accounts/{id}/balance). Method Applies to What it means --- --- --- postings checking, savings, cash, credit cards The stored running balance alone. postings property (a hand-valued asset) Its value is a ledger: a change in value is an entry against equity.revaluation, and reconciling sets the value on a date. See Track a house or other asset. valuation loan The latest valuation replaces the postings sum. A mortgage's feed reports a balance, not a transaction history, so the postings sum is not the debt. postings+holdings brokerage The latest holdings market value is added to the postings sum. Brokerage cash is real money the feed already reported, so it is not discarded. The holdings come from the feed's snapshots or, for an account tracked by hand, from its positions priced at the newest close. When an overlay produced the answer, balance as of names the date of the valuation or snapshot used, and postings balance carries the cash-only figure alongside. Closed accounts always answer from postings: closing zeroes the account, and a stale valuation or snapshot must not resurrect it. Net worth uses these same rules, so an account page and net worth agree.

sections.heading: Two bases, deliberately different
sections.text: There are two ways to ask "what is the balance", and they differ on future-dated rows: - As of a date — GET /accounts/{id}/balance?as of=, MCP account balance. Reads the stored running balance at that date and stops there. A row dated after as of is not counted. - Right now — the accounts list, the account headline, MCP list accounts. Includes every pending and posted row regardless of date, because that is what your bank's "current balance" means. Both apply the same overlays. The difference only shows up when the ledger holds a future-dated row — a pending charge that has not settled, or a scheduled entry you posted early. Forecasts start from the right now basis for exactly this reason: a future-dated pending row must not vanish from a projection.

sections.heading: Balance over time
sections.text: Because a running balance is stored per row, a balance history is a read rather than a computation. GET /accounts/{id}/balance/series?start=&end= returns one point per transaction that moved the account, each carrying the balance after it, the delta, and the transaction id to drill into — plus the opening balance carried into the window, so opening plus every delta equals the last point. The window defaults to the last 90 days. Points are oldest-first. Past 5000 points the response sets truncated rather than quietly dropping the tail. The same three methods apply, and the account type decides once for the whole window — an account does not change how it is valued partway through. The close cutoff, though, applies per date: history before a close keeps its overlay, and from the close date onward the account reads from postings.

sections.heading: Reconciled balances
sections.text: Reconciling an account records a statement balance for a date and posts one adjustment for any difference. It compares against the same chain-head rows the running balance uses, on a basis you choose: posted rows only, or posted plus pending. The claim keeps its target, so every read of the account re-checks it and reports a difference when a later write moved that date's balance. Manual brokerage accounts require component: "cash" and reconcile only cash, excluding securities and unvested awards. Share price changes leave the cash claim unchanged. See Reconcile an account.

sections.heading: Recording a valuation
sections.text: A loan balance is its latest valuation. The feed records one for a synced account; record one yourself with POST /accounts/{id}/valuations, or from an agent with the MCP tool record valuation (both write scope), giving the date and the value on that date. Only loan accounts take a valuation. Any other account is refused with a 422 that says where its balance comes from instead: its transactions, plus its latest holdings snapshot for a brokerage account. A hand-valued asset (type property) is a ledger: record a change or set its value on a date (Track a house or other asset). To bring a checking, savings, cash or credit-card balance to a statement, see Reconcile an account. value is in the ledger's sign by default, the way Purser stores it: positive for something you own, negative for money you owe. To enter a loan figure the way its statement prints it, add "convention": "statement", and Purser negates it exactly as reconciliation does: Account On the date You send Purser stores --- --- --- --- Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "-250000.00" -250000.0000 Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "250000.00", "convention": "statement" -250000.0000 Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "250000.00" rejected with 422 A positive value on a loan is rejected unless you say it is the statement's figure: recorded as given, it would turn the debt into an asset in net worth. The answer's value is always the stored figure, in ledger sign.

sections.heading: For agents
sections.text: Ask search transactions with an account and each row carries balance — the same number the register shows, from that account's perspective. Without an account there is no perspective, so there is no balance field at all; with a category there is none either, since categories are virtual and hold no running balances. For a single point in time use account balance. For a balance over time use balance history(account, period) — one call, not a loop over dates. For a total across rows use spending summary. In no case should you add up amount fields yourself. balance history picks the density itself and tells you what it picked, so a naive call cannot blow your context: 30d is a true daily series, 90d lands on every third day, 1y on every fourteenth. low and high are computed over every day with activity in the window rather than the returned points, so they stay true even when the series is sparse — a low on the 19th is reported correctly by a series that never contains the 19th. movers names the biggest movements. Full per-transaction resolution is behind series uri, which serves exactly the window the tool summarized (for all, the whole history): up to 5000 points, oldest first, with truncated set past that. low and high are end-of-day balances: each day counts with the balance it closed at, never with a value it passed through on the way. Purser orders one day's rows by when they were recorded, not by when the bank processed them, so that order never produces an extreme. A paycheck imported as a gross pay line followed by its same-day tax and benefit deductions is not a high, and a duplicate charge reversed the same day is not a low. The per-transaction points behind series uri still show those intra-day steps. The three questions and their tools: Question Tool --- --- One account, over time balance history(account, period) Everything, over time net worth(period) One account, looking forward forecast balance(account, days) net worth(period="all") starts at the ledger's earliest activity but at most ten years back, and its series uri serves that same window day by day.

sections.heading: Future value on Home
sections.text: Home keeps current owned values prominent in the Net worth and Assets cards. When unvested awards exist, each card adds an Including unvested line; expand Unvested stock in Assets for valuation details. With no unvested awards, the cards show only the current values. The future totals add the current recorded value of unvested stock to owned value, assuming all captured awards vest. These are gross amounts before tax withholding, using recorded stock prices; they do not predict future prices or guaranteed proceeds. Owned balances and the historical net-worth chart continue to count owned assets. Unvested awards enter owned holdings only when a vest is recorded. Closed accounts are excluded from the future view; hidden accounts count. If remaining units or a usable price are missing, Home labels the valuation incomplete and shows the known priced portion. Full future totals stay unknown. Stale prices are identified, with the oldest price date shown. Awards in a non-USD account require currency conversion and leave the total incomplete. The read-only GET /networth/potential endpoint supplies this current snapshot. All sums are calculated by Purser; no balances or awards change when it is read.

pages.title: Categories
pages.description: Why categories are hierarchical virtual accounts rather than tags, how the curated default set works, and how imports arrive already categorized.

sections.text: In Purser a category is not a label you stick on a transaction. It is an account — a virtual one — and categorizing is a real posting to it. That one decision is why spending rollups, transfers, and double-entry all compose cleanly instead of fighting each other.

sections.heading: Categories are virtual accounts
sections.text: There is no categories table. A category is an accounts row with is virtual = true, an income or expense type, and its place in a hierarchy given by an ltree path like expenses.dining.coffee. Because the hierarchy is an ltree, a spending rollup is a single indexed subtree query — everything under expenses.dining is path <@ 'expenses.dining', one query, no recursion in application code. One virtual account is not a category: equity.securities, the other side of a securities trade's cash (see Track holdings by hand). Like a category it is virtual, so it stays out of net worth; unlike one it is never offered as a category, never counted as income or spending, and no rule, schedule or classifier can book to it. The equity subtree belongs to it: no category or account can be created at equity or under it (a 422 says so), and a rollup or spending summary of that subtree counts nothing. A path is labels joined by single dots, each label made of letters, digits, and -. A malformed path such as expenses..dining or expenses.eating out is rejected with a 422 whose message names the offending segment, so a typo never reaches the database.

sections.heading: Why this beats tags
sections.text: A tag is metadata bolted onto a row; nothing balances, and a subtotal means scanning and summing. Making the category an account means the flat write { "category": "expenses.dining" } expands to a balanced posting pair, subtree totals fall out of the ledger itself, and a transfer is just a transaction whose "category" happens to be another real account. Categorization becomes a first-class ledger operation with an audit trail, not an editable sticky note.

sections.heading: A curated, described default set
sections.text: Purser ships 100 categories whose structure is adapted from the Plaid Personal Finance Categories taxonomy, with the transfer and loan-payment groups deliberately removed — those are structural transfers here, not spending. The set is seeded once and merges additively on upgrade, so your deletions stick. Every category carries a one-line description , in Purser's own words, written for the AI classifier and surfaced in Settings - Categories . The set is finite by design . You may rename, re-describe, and add categories, and delete any that are unused, but re-parenting and path renames are not supported in v1. The AI classifier picks from a closed list — the existing tree plus your own accounts in brackets (see below) — and can never invent a category. Agents have no category-creation tool, and creating a category is an admin-UI action, so the taxonomy stays curated rather than sprawling into a thousand near-duplicates. Category paths stay put — schedule templates store them — but a real account can move. PATCH /accounts/{id} with a new path moves it and every account beneath it, keeping their relative paths: a card created at citicard becomes liabilities.citicard. History and balances follow, because transactions point at accounts by id. A destination that another account already occupies is a 409. A destination under a category root such as expenses is refused, because subtree totals there would count the account's own postings as spending. Renaming a real account, in the app or with the MCP update account tool, changes only its display name and keeps its path, so tools, rules and outside integrations that refer to it by path keep working. The name still matters to matching: a bank row that mentions an account's name is one of the signals that links a transfer to it.

sections.heading: Born categorized
sections.text: Imports are not dumped in as uncategorized. A deterministic payee-to-category memory, learned from your accepted history, runs at import time : when Purser has seen a payee before, the new row arrives already categorized, and no correction is ever needed. The optional AI classifier handles only the misses. See design section 11 for that pipeline.

sections.heading: The bracket duality
sections.text: Because a category is an account, the "category" slot is polymorphic. Normally it holds a virtual category account. On a transfer it holds the other real account , shown in Quicken-style brackets like [assets.savings]. Same slot, same flat shape — a categorized expense and a transfer differ only in whether that slot points at a virtual or a real account. See Manage transfers for the write-side sugar. The optional AI classifier can use that slot too: your own accounts are offered to it as bracket options, so a transfer has a correct answer available instead of forcing a wrong category. A bracket answer is one-sided — it names the other account and leaves that side unbacked until the counterparty row arrives — and it must clear a higher confidence bar than an ordinary category, because it restructures the row and moves a second account's balance. Below that bar the row simply stays uncategorized. Collapsing two rows that describe the same movement stays deterministic and is never something the model decides. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md sections 3.2 (categories as virtual accounts), 3.3 (bracket transfers), and 11 (AI categorization).

pages.title: Encryption at rest
pages.description: What Purser encrypts in its database, what it leaves readable and why, how the key is checked and rotated, and what a database dump reveals.

sections.text: Purser encrypts the identifying parts of your financial data inside its database, with a key that never enters the database. This page explains what is encrypted, what is not and why, and what that means for anyone holding a copy of the database. The authoritative specification is DESIGN.md section 9.

sections.heading: The key
sections.text: Encryption is required. Purser uses Fernet: AES-128 in CBC mode for confidentiality, with an HMAC-SHA256 tag so that altered ciphertext is rejected rather than decrypted. The key is PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY, generated with purser keygen. - Every role command needs it. purser serve, purser worker and purser migrate refuse to start when the key is missing or malformed. - It is never stored in the database or in a backup. Purser holds it only in the process environment. The setup wizard shows it once so that you can record it; store it apart from your backups, for example in a password manager. - It can hold several keys. Separate them with commas: the first key encrypts everything new, and any listed key can decrypt. This is how rotation works (below). Losing the key loses the encrypted data. Purser does not start without it, and nothing can decrypt the archived bank data or the descriptive text without it.

sections.heading: The canary: a wrong key fails closed
sections.text: When its migrations first set up the database, Purser stores an encryption canary row: a known value encrypted with the key, and a short fingerprint of the key (a truncated SHA-256 hash, which identifies the key without revealing it). Every start decrypts that row before serving anything. With a wrong key, Purser stops with an error naming the fingerprint the database expects and the fingerprint of the key it was given, instead of running against data it cannot read or, worse, writing new data under a different key.

sections.heading: What is encrypted
sections.text: Purser encrypts each value in the application before it reaches PostgreSQL, and decrypts it only when a request or job needs it. Encrypted values are never written to logs. - Bank data: the archive of every payload received from the bank feed, and the SimpleFIN access URLs, which are the credentials to your bank data. - Descriptive text (the "narrative layer"): payee names, transaction descriptions, posting memos, schedule names, review notes, financial notes, rules' match text, payee names and notes, suggestion drafts, evidence and decision notes, the notes and history on bill estimates, and the notes, plans and references on hand-tracked holdings, tax lots and equity awards. - Audit and events: the before and after detail of audit entries, the recorded authorization details of tokens, and the payloads of the event stream. - Secrets: webhook signing secrets, and the secret settings (the AI provider API key, the OIDC client secret and the price provider API key), which are also write-only through the API.

sections.heading: What stays readable, and why
sections.text: The numbers stay plaintext: amounts, dates, statuses, currencies, balances, category and account paths, account names, holdings and prices, and the ids that link records. Every total, balance, forecast and ledger check is computed by the database on these columns, and PostgreSQL cannot compute on values only the application can decrypt. For the same reason, a direct database reader, such as a reporting connection, sees these columns and only ciphertext for the encrypted ones. User emails and display names are also plaintext. Passwords and API tokens are stored as one-way hashes, not encrypted values.

sections.heading: What a database dump reveals
sections.text: Assume someone has a dump of the database but not the key. They can see: - your accounts, their names and structure, and their balances over time; - every transaction's amount, date and category, so how much you spend in each category and when; - your holdings, prices and net worth; - schedules' amounts and timing, without their names; - which transactions share a payee, without the payee's name. They cannot read who you paid, what a transaction was for, your notes, the bank's original records, your bank credentials or your secrets. Treat a dump as sensitive financial data all the same: write it readable only by you and keep it somewhere private.

sections.heading: Searching and deduplicating encrypted data
sections.text: Two things must still work on encrypted text: finding a payee by name, and recognising a transaction that has already been imported. - A blind index stores a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of each normalized payee name next to the encrypted name. Purser finds a payee by computing the same hash, without decrypting every row. Equal names have equal hashes, which is why a dump shows which transactions share a payee. - Each transaction's content hash , which makes imports idempotent, is keyed the same way. Without the key, someone holding a dump cannot confirm a guessed transaction (a date, an amount and a description) by hashing it. - The stable payee references given to agents when payee names are withheld (py ..., see Privacy and agents) are keyed hashes too. These hashes use three separate random keys, one per purpose, each stored in the database wrapped (encrypted) by PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY. Because they are random rather than derived from your key, rotating your key only rewraps them: every index, content hash and payee reference stays byte-identical. Substring search in descriptions works by decrypting the candidate rows in the application, after the database has narrowed them by account, date and status.

sections.heading: Rotating the key
sections.text: Rotate with the guarded purser admin rotate-key command, run with the new key first and the old key second in PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY. It re-encrypts every encrypted value under the new key in one transaction, without exposing the plaintext, and moves the canary to the new key. Then remove the old key from the variable. See Rotate the encryption key and the CLI reference.

sections.heading: What Purser does not protect
sections.text: Encryption at rest protects copies of the database: dumps, backups and stolen database files. It does not protect against: - Someone with the key. Anyone who can read your .env file or the container's environment (for example with docker inspect) holds the key. Restrict who can administer the host. - A token or a signed-in session. Purser decrypts data for whoever is authorized to read it. What an agent receives is governed by scopes and disclosure settings, not by encryption. - The plaintext columns on disk. Encrypting the disk or the volume that holds the database, and the disks that hold your backups, is outside Purser's control and still recommended.

pages.title: Forecasting
pages.description: Why Purser forecasts deterministically from schedules and running balances, with no statistical models, and how shortfalls surface.

sections.text: Purser's forecast answers "will this account dip below zero before payday?" and it answers it the same way every time. The forecast is deterministic : it is your current balance plus the expected transactions your schedules already imply -- not a prediction learned from a model.

sections.heading: Schedules plus running balances
sections.text: A forecast starts from a real, stored balance and walks forward, applying each expected instance that active schedules materialize on the horizon. The result is a daily series where every step is a named, dated event — the rent on the 1st, the paycheck on the 15th — carrying the running balance after at that point. The narration and the chart come from exactly the same data, because the events array is the chart.

sections.heading: No statistical models, by design
sections.text: There is no regression, no seasonality model, no machine-learned trend. That is a choice, not a gap. A deterministic forecast is explainable : every projected movement traces to a schedule you can inspect and edit, so when the number surprises you, you can see precisely which expectation caused it. A statistical forecast that is confidently wrong about your rent is worse than useless for planning cash.

sections.heading: Shortfalls
sections.text: forecast balance(account, days) (horizon defaults to 30 days) returns the daily series, the projected minimum (low), and the account floor (min balance, null when unset; the headline then measures against zero). Calling it only reads: it never emits an event. The warning comes from a nightly scan instead. At 07:15 UTC Purser forecasts the next 30 days of every open account that has a floor, and when a projection crosses that floor it emits a forecast.shortfall event, once per account and first shortfall date. The warning reaches you through the event stream, a webhook, or the whats new digest before the account actually runs dry, not after. An account without a floor is never scanned, so set one on every account you want watched. The floor is the account's min balance, a decimal string in ledger sign. Set it when you create the account (POST /accounts) or at any time after: the Set floor control in the account's register header, PATCH /accounts/{id} with {"min balance": "500.00"}, or the MCP tool update account(account, min balance="500.00"), so an agent can act on "warn me if checking goes under $500". Changing it needs the write scope, like a rename, and is audited as an account.update with the old and new floor. The next nightly scan uses the new floor. Clearing it (null over REST, "" in update account, Clear in the app) takes the account out of the scan, so its warnings stop. A credit card is negative when owed, so "warn me past 4,500.00 owed" is a floor of -4500.00; zero warns before an overdraft. Floors apply to checking, savings, cash and credit-card accounts. Brokerage, property and loan forecasts start from a market value or a stated valuation, so a floor there is refused (422).

sections.heading: Horizon semantics
sections.text: The horizon is a count of days forward from today, up to 365. Schedules materialize their instances on a rolling 60-day window; for slots past that the forecaster expands the rules on the fly, so a 180-day call still shows every occurrence. Those events are flagged projected — the rule expects them, but no instance row exists yet to edit or match — while events with a transaction id are instances you can skip, override or mark paid. An instance dated before today that has not been matched is flagged overdue: it lands on day 0, because it is still due. The uncleared rows of a file import are expected too, so an outstanding check lands on day 0 the same way until the matcher pairs it with the bank's posted row. A slot you skipped never appears, projected or not. The series stays daily, and the full daily series is always available behind a purser:// resource. An instance the matcher has already proposed a bank row for is treated as paid, pending your confirmation. That row — pending or posted — is already in the starting balance, so landing the instance as well would subtract the money twice. The forecast leaves it out, whether it is overdue or due within the five-day match window, and the line is exactly what confirming the match would give: the bank's amount, never a leftover difference. Reject the proposal and the instance is back on the next forecast; confirm it (in the register, or with match on the same pair) and it is settled for good. An account valued by a stated figure rather than its postings (a loan with a valuation) keeps such instances, because no bank row moves that figure.

sections.heading: Where each amount comes from
sections.text: Every event carries a basis: what produced its amount. A schedule's own amount is fixed, or the estimate it follows — last, rolling avg 3, rolling avg 12, or counterparty balance, which for a card payment is the card's current balance. An amount someone supplied is override (you pinned the instance with a different amount or date) or statement (a recorded card statement balance). The REST forecast and the full daily series carry basis on every event; forecast balance names it only for statement and override, the amounts an agent should be able to explain, and leaves it off the rest to stay inside its budget.

sections.heading: Estimate range
sections.text: An estimated amount is a point taken from history, and history varies. So an event whose amount a schedule estimates — a rolling average, the last amount, or a card payment's current balance — also carries a range: the lowest and highest of the schedule's six newest settled amounts together with the event's own amount, so the point always sits inside. A card payment's range is its past payments together with the card's current balance (not the balance's swing from zero to its peak over a cycle). It needs at least two settled amounts that differ; a fixed amount, an amount you overrode, and a recorded card statement have no range, because nothing about them is uncertain. When any event has a range, the forecast also walks the horizon twice more: once with every ranged event at its worst (outflows at their high, inflows at their low) and once at its best. Each day then carries low and high beside its balance, and the forecast reports the lowest point of each pass. forecast balance puts that under low.range — low and low date for the pessimistic pass, high for the optimistic one — and when only the pessimistic pass dips below the floor, the headline says which event would cause it: "It could dip to -125.00 on 2026-10-26 if Citi payment comes in high." The forecast.shortfall event stays on the expected amounts, so a wide range never raises an alert on its own. The forecast widget and the Scheduled transactions page chart shade the band behind the line, and an event's tooltip names its basis and range.

sections.heading: What the event list shows
sections.text: forecast balance keeps its answer inside a token budget, so its events list holds the movements that fit, not necessarily all of them. The movement that produces the projected low is always listed, then the largest by amount; pass materiality (a decimal string such as "100.00") to list only movements at least that large. Whatever is not listed is accounted for in omitted — how many movements and their net — and end balance is the balance on the last day, so start balance plus the listed amounts plus omitted.net is always end balance. truncated is true only when the budget, rather than your materiality, left a movement out, and the headline then says how many. Every day is in the series the payload's daily uri names: read it with resources/read, or with the read series tool when your client or gateway forwards tools but not resources. The horizon (days) is 1 to 365, and every horizon the tool accepts is one the series serves.

sections.heading: Coverage: what the line is made of
sections.text: Every forecast carries coverage: how many active schedules touch the account, how many instances and projected occurrences went into the line, how many open suggestions name the account, and matches pending — how many instances were left out as paid pending a match confirmation, with their net in matches pending net (a decimal string, present only when it is not zero). The headline names them too, so a caller knows confirmations are outstanding: list unmatched shows each one with proposed posted id, the bank row it was paired with, and match on that pair confirms it. A flat line with schedules active: 0 is not a calm month — it is an account with nothing modeled, and the headline says so instead of reporting that the balance "stays above its floor". Looking backward is the mirror image. One account's history is balance history(account, period), which reads the same kind of recorded running balance in the other direction — and has the same "the series IS the chart" property, except the numbers were stored rather than projected. Net worth over time is the whole-portfolio counterpart — see design section 8. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 6 (schedules and forecasting). The tool contract is in the MCP tool catalog under forecast balance.

sections.heading: Independent amount and date uncertainty
sections.text: Forecast events carry the same per-occurrence certainty shown in Scheduled transactions, including rule-only projected events. The Estimate badge explains whether amount, date or both remain estimated. Confirmed upcoming events remain scheduled until matched; confirmation itself does not post money. A confirmed amount has no historical amount range even if its date is still uncertain. The full REST forecast and daily MCP resource include the evidence and original snapshot. Compact forecast balance events keep the uncertainty status and true-only amount estimated / date estimated flags (omitted means false). Supplied amounts also name their statement or override basis; get schedule occurrence reads detailed provenance for a materialized transaction id. All structured amounts and variances use the forecast account's perspective, including a transfer's opposite leg. Proposed matches remain pending review while retaining the existing forecast suppression rules above. A fixed calculated value can still be an estimate. Projected events expose certainty.slot (schedule and recurrence date), so evidence does not require a materialized transaction. Annotating that slot changes certainty only; the event amount, date, calculation basis and daily balances stay the same. Evidence and the first retained projection follow the occurrence when it materializes. See projected-slot evidence for the metadata-only migration path.

pages.title: The ledger
pages.description: Balanced postings, correction history, source records and reconciliation.

sections.text: Purser checks that transaction postings balance, preserves the history of corrections and archives imported source data. Reconciliation compares ledger balances with statements. These checks detect inconsistencies; they do not guarantee that source data or categorization is correct.

sections.heading: Flat outside, double-entry inside
sections.text: Clients — human or agent — submit the flat form a person thinks in: { "account": "citicard", "date": "2026-07-01", "amount": "-14.00", "payee": "Chipotle", "category": "expenses.dining" } The server expands every write into a balanced posting pair (citicard -14.00, expenses.dining +14.00). Postings per transaction sum to zero per currency — enforced in the application layer with a database trigger as backstop. Reads return the flat view by default; full postings are available on request. Categories are themselves accounts — hierarchical virtual accounts with ltree paths like expenses.dining.coffee — which is what makes categorization a first-class ledger operation instead of a tag. A transfer is one transaction with two real-account postings; in the flat view its "category" appears as the other account in Quicken-style brackets, like [assets.savings]. A split loan payment keeps both bank legs exact and adds one interest/fee posting for the difference, so it still sums to zero — see Confirm a split loan payment.

sections.heading: Split transactions
sections.text: One bank amount spread over several categories is a split transaction : one leg on the real account plus one leg per category line, still summing to zero. It is never a transfer and never has a second real leg; money a split sends to another account is a transfer of its own. The flat view shows a split with no single category path and a split lines count, and the transaction's postings carry the lines. Split rows come from QIF imports today and are read-only.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and immutability
sections.text: Every transaction moves through expected - pending - posted - void: - expected — future entries: manual bills, materialized schedule instances, and the rows a QIF or CSV file marks uncleared. Estimates, consumed by the matcher and forecaster. - pending — rows the bank feed reports as not yet cleared, and manual or agent entries the bank has not posted yet. Freely editable. - posted — immutable . Any change, including recategorization, executes as an atomic reversal + replacement pair linked via reverses id. The flat view collapses the chain; the ledger keeps the forensic history. The database allows exactly one mutation of a posted row: voiding it with a lineage link in the same statement. - void — dead rows kept for lineage: superseded expecteds, merged transfer halves, vanished pendings, reversal legs. Corrections to posted transactions are recorded as ledger events with an audit trail. In the admin app's register, changing a posted row's category is just that: there is no confirmation step. The corrected row shows Corrected · Undo , and Undo puts the previous category back the only way a posted row allows, as one more reversal + replacement. Both corrections stay in the ledger and the audit log.

sections.heading: The raw feed underneath
sections.text: Every payload a bank connection returns is archived verbatim, append-only, before anything touches the ledger. Feed syncs and manual imports are content-hash idempotent — re-running any import produces zero new rows. A row's identity is what the bank sent (account, date, amount, description) plus, for identical rows in one payload, which occurrence it is — so two same-day coffees at the same price stay two rows, and re-fetching or re-importing them adds none. Imported rows retain links to their source records. Manual entries and later corrections have their own audit history; bank payloads alone do not contain those decisions.

sections.heading: Where the invariants live
sections.text: These rules are enforced structurally — app-layer checks with database triggers as backstop, and property-based tests over the invariants (zero-sum postings, immutability, idempotent import). The authoritative specification is DESIGN.md in the repository — these pages explain the behavior; that document defines it.

pages.title: Matching
pages.description: How expected payments are matched to bank transactions, with candidate scoring and recorded variances.

sections.text: Purser matches expected payments to bank transactions. Expectations include manual bills, schedule instances and uncleared rows from a file import. Matching retains the bank-reported amount and records differences from the estimate.

sections.heading: Expected versus imported
sections.text: An expected transaction is an estimate: the $60.00 gym charge you know is coming. An imported pending or posted row is what the feed reported. The matcher's job is to recognize that these two are the same event and collapse them into one truthful row — without ever letting the estimate overwrite what really happened.

sections.heading: Candidate scoring
sections.text: For each expectation the matcher looks at rows in the same account within a date window (default plus or minus 5 days), scoring normalized-payee similarity and amount closeness. Crucially, amount is weighted softly : a row whose payee and date agree but whose amount differs is still a confident match — it just carries a variance . That is deliberate. A subscription that quietly rose from "-9.99" to "-11.99" should still match its schedule, and the price change should be recorded , not hidden by a failure to match. Candidates are bank reality: imported rows, and any live transfer — the two-leg row the auto-linker (or your confirm) builds when both sides of a card payment arrive. Every row is scored through the account being matched : a one-leg import and a two-leg transfer are both "-500.00 on checking" from checking's point of view. An expected transfer (a schedule with a counterparty account) is tried from each of its two accounts, and two rows that name the same counterparty account count as agreeing on the payee — which is how the expected card payment pairs with a merged transfer that carries no payee.

sections.heading: Three tiers
sections.text: The score sorts each expectation into one of three outcomes: - auto — a high score matches automatically only when the occurrence is not estimated and the candidate is unambiguous. - proposed — a middling score becomes a proposed match for you to confirm or reject. It waits as a match card in the suggestions inbox, and in the account register. Rejecting it is remembered: the matcher never proposes — or matches on its own — that bank row for that bill again, nor the posted row that replaces it. You can still mark the bill paid with it by hand. - unmatched — a low score leaves both rows standing.

sections.heading: Posted amount wins, and supersede
sections.text: When a match is made, the expectation is voided with a superseded by link to the posted row, and the posted amount is truth. The flat view collapses the pair to the single real transaction; the ledger keeps the forensic lineage. The matches row records the score and the variance, and that variance is not discarded — it sharpens future schedule estimates and, past a threshold, emits a variance.threshold event. A match can name a pending row, and pending rows are not final. When the feed replaces a pending with its posted row, a confirmed match moves to the posted row and a proposal is decided again. When the bank drops the pending, the match is released and the expectation comes back, because a dropped charge paid nothing. Voiding a matched pending yourself works the same way: the match is released (a proposal is withdrawn) and the expectation is due again. Estimates read only posted rows, and they read the current version of each: the posted successor of a pending, the transfer a row was merged into, the replacement of a corrected row.

sections.heading: Transfers whose sides post on different days
sections.text: The two bank legs of a transfer rarely post together, and the nightly job matches before it links transfers. When only the first leg has arrived, an expected transfer can settle against it — the matcher sees that leg from the account being matched, so it is a fair candidate (proposed when only the amount and date agree). That does not lock the leg away. A bank row matched to an expected transfer stays available for pairing, but only with a row on the transfer's other account, and when its counterpart arrives and the two link, the match follows the bank line into the merged transfer: a confirmed match simply moves, and a proposal is decided again against the merge, which agrees on accounts, amount and date. The expectation is settled exactly once, by the transfer, and the merged transfer — now matched — settles nothing else. A row matched to an ordinary bill never takes part. Unlinking the transfer releases what it settled, so the expectation is due again rather than settled by a row that no longer exists.

sections.heading: Unmatched, both directions
sections.text: The gaps are reported both ways, with aging: expected-but-missing rows are late bills, and posted-but-unexpected rows are new spending to triage. The list unmatched tool answers each direction, so an agent can ask "what bills haven't shown up?" and "what did I spend that I didn't plan?" as one call each. Transfer detection is a specialized branch of the same machinery — see Manage transfers. A pair that looks like a transfer but carries nothing to link it waits for you the way a proposed match does: as a transfer pair card in the inbox, and rejecting it is remembered by every automatic path. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 5, and the principle behind it is design principle 5. Correction history contributes only its current replacement. A reversal is an accounting entry, not a bank payment, and cannot settle an expected bill.

sections.heading: Occurrence certainty and review
sections.text: Amount and date estimates are tracked independently. An estimated dimension cannot make a plausible candidate certain: estimated occurrences require review. Two candidates within 0.10 of the best score, or competing recurrence slots for the same movement, also require review. Account, direction, currency and counterparty compatibility are checked even for manual confirmation. The original estimate and its provenance remain available beside the linked actual and amount/timing variance. Unmatching keeps confirmation evidence on the replacement occurrence; reset explicitly returns it to the rule. It never creates another posted transaction. See Occurrence estimates.

pages.title: Financial notes
pages.description: Save notes about your finances in Purser for your agent to use as context.

sections.text: Financial notes keep information alongside your records that transactions alone cannot explain: "the HOA bill is annual," "this transfer is a 529 contribution," or "pay this card from checking." Your agent can retrieve these notes as context in later sessions. The API calls these records memories . The existing /memories endpoints, list memories, propose memory and archive memory tools manage them. In the admin UI, they appear under Settings → Agent memory , where you record a note and tick the accounts it is about (none ticked: it applies everywhere).

sections.heading: Notes and rules
sections.text: Notes store context; they are not executable rules. Saving a note does not change a ledger entry. A connected agent, or an optional model integration, can use the text when deciding what to do. For automatic categorization or payee renaming, use a rule. Rules can cite a note, but archiving that note does not disable the rule.

sections.heading: Where they show up
sections.text: - describe() returns the active-note count and a bounded set of pinned notes. - list memories retrieves notes, optionally filtered by account, category or payee. - The review loop attaches notes relevant to the transaction being reviewed. - Optional AI categorization , when configured, receives relevant notes as prompt context.

sections.heading: Relevance
sections.text: Notes can link to accounts, categories or payees. Filtering uses those exact links. Notes with no links apply globally. At categorization time, the category is still being decided, so the classifier uses account and payee links. A note linked only to a category will not reach it. Link to the relevant account or payee when you want it used there.

sections.heading: Drafts and activation
sections.text: When an agent proposes a note, it starts as a draft unless you explicitly asked the agent to save it as active context. You can approve drafts in Settings → Agent memory . Drafts are excluded from describe(), ordinary listings, review context and classifier prompts. Listings can request them explicitly with include drafts for inspection. Purser allows up to 500 characters per note, 100 active notes, 8 pinned notes and 25 drafts.

sections.heading: Response limits
sections.text: describe() includes at most 8 pinned notes and 1,000 characters. list memories returns at most 25 notes and 2,500 characters per call. Classifier context includes at most 5 notes. Listing responses report omitted counts when a limit truncates the result.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Note text is encrypted at rest. Reading notes requires read scope; creating or updating them requires write. MCP disclosure defaults also apply to notes: with purchase privacy enabled, known payee names in the text are replaced with references unless requested. See Privacy and agents.

sections.heading: Archiving
sections.text: Archiving removes a note from active context and can be reversed. Hard deletion requires admin access. Its audit record remains only for the configured retention period. Purser does not automatically edit or archive notes. If all of a note's linked accounts are closed or hidden, Purser flags it as stale for review.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: - Write deterministic rules - Review new transactions - DESIGN.md section 3.6 and decision 48

pages.title: Privacy and agents
pages.description: Control financial data sharing through access scopes, MCP disclosure defaults, per-call requests and auditing.

sections.text: You decide what financial information to share with your AI agent. Purser provides access scopes, disclosure defaults and an audit log. It does not prescribe how much information you should share. Data returned to an agent may enter its model's context; where that data goes depends on the agent and provider you use. Token scopes control which operations are allowed. MCP disclosure settings control which fields are returned by default. An agent with read access can request omitted fields per call without another approval step. These settings are not field-level access restrictions. For scope details, see Security model. The authoritative spec is design section 9.

sections.heading: Two settings
sections.text: Both are in Settings - Agents & API , under Privacy with agents , and both are off by default (PURSER PRIVACY PURCHASE, PURSER PRIVACY AMOUNT; see Configuration). Setting What an agent receives --- --- Privatize the purchase Each payee as a stable reference such as py 8k2mq4x7ra instead of its name. Descriptions, posting memos and bill (schedule) names are left out. Accounts and categories stay, because their names are yours and they carry most of the meaning. Privatize the amount No single-transaction amount: no row amount, no posting amount, no running balance (it would give each row's amount away by subtraction), no individual bill or forecast-event amount. Totals stay exact whatever the settings: spending summary totals, account balance, net worth, balance history series and the forecast's end balance. When an agent asks for a total, the total is the answer. Amounts are exact or left out, never rounded or made up: a number that is not true is something an agent might reason from or repeat. External account identifiers (the bank's account ids and connection ids) are left out for agents by default, whatever the settings. A call that passes include: ["external ids"] gets them.

sections.heading: Every omission is named
sections.text: A response says what it withheld, for example "withheld": ["amount", "payee"]. An agent that saw a field simply missing would conclude the value is unknown and might try to fix it.

sections.heading: Asking for a field: include
sections.text: A setting is a default, not a limit. Every tool that can return a withheld field takes include, any of payee, description, amount and external ids, and returns exactly those fields on that call. The audit log separately records additional fields requested and fields observed in the final response. Open Settings - Audit log Data shared for all integration reads, including ordinary reads within the defaults and aggregate answers. Only fields returned beyond privacy defaults narrows the view to observed extra fields; it is not a list of all sharing. Failed or empty requests do not prove those fields were returned. Some free-text responses have only a partial field inventory. Authorization means the integration has permission to act. It does not mean the user approved each individual read. The log identifies the credential Purser served; downstream model providers and forwarding are not verified. For evidence, retention and capture failures, see Security.

sections.heading: Working by reference
sections.text: Payee references and transaction ids work as inputs everywhere a payee or a row is named: search transactions(payee=...), update transaction, propose rule, match, links on financial notes. Purser resolves them. A payee name you typed yourself is still accepted as a filter, because you disclosed it, not Purser; the answer stays privatized. A reference is never accepted inside free text (a description, a memo, a note, a name), so a reference cannot turn into a payee's real name. A reference stays the same when the encryption key is rotated, so an agent's long-term notes about it stay valid.

sections.heading: Showing you the details: present
sections.text: present(transaction ids, note) returns a link that opens those rows, with full detail, in Purser for you when you are signed in. The agent can reply "your four largest charges this week" followed by the link and the values never pass through its model. The link carries only transaction ids and the note.

sections.heading: MCP, REST and the web UI
sections.text: These settings govern what Purser hands an agent over MCP. Purser's own web pages always show you full detail. REST serves full detail to any token that can read, except external account identifiers, which it leaves out for API tokens without admin scope.

pages.title: Security model
pages.description: Access scopes, audit logs, correction history, sign-in throttling and encryption at rest.

sections.text: Purser controls access through token scopes and records reads and writes in an audit log. Posted transactions retain correction history. This page covers those controls, sign-in protection and encryption; the authoritative spec is design section 9.

sections.heading: Scopes
sections.text: Every token carries one or more scopes: Scope Grants --- --- read Financial reads: transactions, ledger and bank balances, reports, tools and resources. write Every write: transactions, matches, transfers, rules, schedules, suggestions, valuations, holdings. admin Token and configuration management. The recommended default for an agent is read + write . Account read access includes the bank-reported balance, available balance, freshness and comparison basis, as well as transactions and the ledger balance. Use GET /accounts/{id}, GET /accounts/{id}/balance or MCP account balance; each includes bank snapshot. Permissions currently apply across the instance; there are no per-account or per-tenant access lists. Connection discovery is a configuration surface and remains admin-only, as do credentials, setup and mapping. Reading an account's bank balances does not require that access. The bank snapshot never includes credentials, bank account numbers or provider identifiers, even for an administrator.

sections.heading: Undo, not pre-approval
sections.text: The safety net for an agent's writes is undo, not a review queue in front of every change. Posted transactions are immutable: a correction is a linked reversal pair, so nothing an agent does erases history. Every write is recorded in the audit log against the token that made it, and the register marks agent-made rows as agent-made. Proposing is the agent's choice per call. When it carries out your request, it writes directly. When it acts on its own initiative — a pattern it noticed, a rule it thinks would help — it proposes instead: a rule or a financial note stays a draft that never runs or is served until you activate it, and a schedule lands as a suggestion for you to decide. A note stays a draft unless you asked the agent to remember something, because an active note can be served as context in future sessions. Every endpoint and tool declares the scope it requires; no route is open by default. The few that answer without a token are deliberate: first-run setup (until the first administrator exists), /healthz and /llms.txt.

sections.heading: What an agent sees
sections.text: You choose the agent, its access scopes and your disclosure defaults. Data returned to an agent may enter its model's context. Two MCP settings (Settings, Agents & API, off by default) omit purchase details and individual amounts. An agent can request those fields per call; the audit log records those requests. These defaults do not restrict which fields a readable tool can disclose. External account identifiers are omitted by default from MCP responses. See Privacy and agents for the settings and the differences between MCP, REST and browser access.

sections.heading: No self-escalation for non-admin tokens
sections.text: POST /tokens requires admin scope. A non-admin agent token cannot mint a copy of itself or grant itself stronger scopes. An admin-scoped API token can create tokens , just as an admin's browser session can. Reserve that scope for trusted administration; it does not distinguish a human caller from automation.

sections.heading: Who can revoke a token
sections.text: Any token can revoke itself. A person signed in to the web UI sees and revokes every token of their own account under Settings - Agents & API : their other sessions, and, for the admin, every agent token, since agent tokens are created under the admin's account. An admin-scoped token can revoke any token. Any other agent token sees only itself in GET /tokens and can revoke only itself. A request to revoke any other token gets the same 404 as a token that does not exist, so a leaked read-only token can neither sign the admin out, nor cut off the other agents, nor confirm that another token exists.

sections.heading: Reads are audited too
sections.text: The audit log ( Settings - Audit log ) opens on Data shared : what Purser returned to an authorized integration, the accounts and dates identified in the response, fields withheld, and the outcome. Changes made , Access & permissions , and Technical activity keep mutations, grants and browser/system activity available separately. Expand an entry for its authorization, evidence ID and linked activity. Response summaries show recorded categories and counts; empty category, account and withheld-field summaries are omitted. Recorded field paths remain available under Technical details , even when no category was assigned. Filters run on the server across the retained history, not just loaded entries. Use Load older entries to continue, or Export CSV/JSON for every matching entry. Filter URLs can be bookmarked. Dates show the browser's local timezone; export timestamps include their UTC offset. Account, data-type and extra-field filters require recorded evidence, so they cannot match older entries that lack it. New records contain a field inventory and counts, not a copy of financial values. An inventory can be partial when a response includes free text or exceeds inventory limits. Requested coverage is separate from dates actually found in the response. Historical entries explicitly state that detailed sharing information was not recorded. They do not acquire guessed authorization or response data on upgrade. An integration's response is recorded before Purser releases it. If capture fails, Purser withholds the response: REST returns 503 and MCP returns an error. A write may already have completed; check its state before retrying. REST integration responses above 16 MiB are withheld with 413; narrow the request. Browser activity remains best-effort so an administrator can investigate an audit outage. A separate completion record identifies an HTTP send or an MCP result returned to the transport. Missing completion evidence appears as Delivery uncertain . Purser cannot prove that a client received the data or where it forwarded it. Capture-failure notices describe the current server process since its start, not all servers or historical uptime. Each mutation retains its before/after entry, linked to the call by request ID. Audit access and exports require admin scope. Sensitive audit details and grant snapshots are encrypted. Retention is finite and uniform (audit retention days, default 90, floor 7), pruned nightly, including completion records. The page shows the configured duration and earliest retained entry. The durable event stream is separate.

sections.heading: Sign-in throttling
sections.text: Password sign-in is throttled against online guessing. Failures are counted per email and per client address: after five in a row for one email, or twenty from one address, further attempts are refused with 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header — before the password is even checked, so a locked-out guesser learns nothing. The lockout starts at 30 seconds and doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes. A successful sign-in clears its email's count; the address count only fades with time, so one valid password cannot cover a spray across other accounts. Every failed and every throttled attempt is audited (auth.login failed, auth.login throttled) with the email as entered and the client address — never the password. A refused sign-in never says whether an account exists. An unknown email gets the same 401 as a wrong password, and it takes as long: when there is no password to check, Purser checks the guess against a stand-in hash, so the response time gives nothing away either. The counts live in memory, per process: a restart clears them, and each API replica keeps its own. SSO sign-in and agent tokens never pass through it. The limits, and the proxy setting that lets the per-address count see real clients, are in Configuration.

sections.heading: Single sign-on
sections.text: SSO uses the OpenID Connect authorization code flow with state, nonce and PKCE, and validates the id token before any account lookup: an RS256 or ES256 signature from the provider's published keys, then issuer, audience, expiry and nonce. An SSO identity is the provider together with its subject. A provider's email links to an existing account, or creates one, only when the provider asserts it is verified, and an auto-created account is a member, never an admin. An account linked to one identity refuses another identity from the same provider until an admin unlinks it; a verified email moves it to a different provider. Emails match regardless of letter case. Only an admin can change the SSO settings, and password sign-in stays available whatever they say. The full list of checks is in Single sign-on with OIDC.

sections.heading: Requests from other sites
sections.text: The web UI signs you in with a session cookie, and a browser sends that cookie with any request to Purser, even one a page elsewhere triggers. So a write made with the cookie is refused (403) when the browser reports that another page sent it (Sec-Fetch-Site, or Origin). Reads, agent tokens and scripts are not affected. Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES), so no request, signed in or not, can make the server hold more.

sections.heading: Encryption at rest
sections.text: Encryption is required: Purser refuses to start without PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY, and a canary row makes a wrong key fail closed at startup. Descriptive text (payees, descriptions, memos, notes, audit detail), the archived bank data, bank credentials and secrets are encrypted; amounts, dates, statuses, category paths and ids stay plaintext so the database can compute on them. Keyed hashes keep search and deduplication working without letting a database dump confirm a guessed transaction. See Encryption at rest for the full model, what a dump reveals, and key rotation.

sections.heading: The raw archive underneath
sections.text: Beneath the ledger, every bank payload is archived to raw fetches append-only, before anything touches the books — no code path may update or delete it. The ledger is a projection that can always be re-derived from those bytes, which is the last line of the trust story: even the ledger cannot quietly diverge from what the bank actually sent. See The ledger. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 9.

sections.heading: First administrator
sections.text: Complete setup before exposing a new instance to other users. The setup endpoint is intentionally unauthenticated until the first administrator exists. Concurrent setup attempts serialize through a PostgreSQL transaction lock, so exactly one can create the first administrator even when multiple API processes run. Later attempts receive 409 Conflict; a failed transaction releases the lock.

sections.heading: Reporting bugs and vulnerabilities
sections.text: - Bugs and feature requests: open an issue at github.com/mlamoure/purser/issues. Use synthetic data in examples; never paste real account numbers, tokens, access URLs or encryption keys. - Pull requests are welcome. Purser is developed in a separate repository and published to GitHub as one commit per release, so a pull request is not merged as is: the maintainer applies the change upstream and it ships in the next release. - Security vulnerabilities: report privately with Report a vulnerability on the repository's Security tab, never in a public issue. Fixes land in the latest release, the only supported version.

pages.title: Backup and restore
pages.description: Back up the single Postgres database, keep the encryption key safe separately, rotate keys, and run a restore drill.

sections.text: Purser keeps everything — ledger, append-only raw archive, config, audit — in one PostgreSQL database . Backup and restore are therefore ordinary Postgres operations, with one rule that matters more than any other.

sections.heading: The one rule: the key is not in the backup
sections.text: Data at rest is encrypted, and PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY is not stored in the database. A database dump contains ciphertext and the wrapped data-encryption keys, but not the master key that unwraps them. A backup is useless without the key. Record the key separately — a password manager, not the same bucket as your dumps — or your archived bank history is unrecoverable. This is the same key the setup wizard reveals at install (or Settings - Security , if setup was interrupted), until you acknowledge that you have recorded it.

sections.heading: Back up
sections.text: umask 077 the dump is readable by you alone pg dump --format=custom --file=purser-2026-07-17.dump \ "postgresql://purser@db.example.com:5432/purser" Amounts, dates and account names are plaintext in a dump (see below), so keep dumps private: umask 077 before writing one, and a private bucket for copies. That single dump is the whole instance. Store the encryption key alongside your records of where the dumps live — never inside them.

sections.heading: What is and is not encrypted
sections.text: A dump holds ciphertext for the archived bank data, SimpleFIN access URLs, secrets and descriptive text (payees, descriptions, memos, notes, audit detail), and plaintext for amounts, dates, statuses, account names, category paths and ids. Encrypting the database files and the disks that hold your dumps is outside Purser's control. See Encryption at rest for the complete list and what a dump reveals.

sections.heading: Rotate the encryption key
sections.text: Rotate with the guarded CLI. Run with both keys configured — the new one first — so ciphertext re-wraps under the new key without ever exposing plaintext, and blind indexes and content hashes stay byte-identical: export PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY="<new-key ,<old-key " purser admin rotate-key Then drop the old key from the variable. See purser admin rotate-key for detail.

sections.heading: Restore drill
sections.text: Practice this before you need it: 1. Provision an empty PostgreSQL 16 database. 2. Before restoring into a fresh cluster, create the database owner/login used by the application and the read-model role: CREATE ROLE purser read NOLOGIN;. A database dump does not include cluster roles. If this role already exists, preserve it. Restore any separately managed reporting login configuration from your secure operational records; do not enable a new login by default. 3. pg restore --exit-on-error --dbname=... purser-2026-07-17.dump. 4. Start Purser with the same PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY set on the process (PURSER DATABASE URL pointing at the restored database). At startup Purser checks an encryption canary row that binds the key to the database: a wrong or missing key fails closed before serving anything, naming both fingerprints. A clean GET /healthz ({"status":"ok","database":"ok"}) confirms startup and database connectivity, not the completeness of a restore. Compare account balances and historical totals with the original instance, open encrypted descriptions, check record counts and raw archives, and verify that importing the same data again creates no duplicates. Do not treat health alone as proof that your financial data has been recovered.

sections.heading: Upgrade and roll back
sections.text: Upgrades move the database schema forward, and there is no downgrade. Your rollback point is a backup taken before the upgrade, together with the image you were running and the same key. 1. Note the image you run now (the exact tag or digest), and keep your key. 2. Take a backup (see Back up) and check it restores, ideally into a scratch database. 3. Change the image to the new version and restart. With Docker Compose, download the new release's docker-compose.yml (its URL carries the release tag, as in the Quickstart) over the old one in the same directory, keeping .env, then run docker compose pull and docker compose up -d. Migrations run automatically at startup. The API (serve) and the worker may start at the same time: they take turns on a database lock, so the migration runs once. 4. Check the instance as in the restore drill: balances, historical totals and encrypted descriptions match what you saw before. To roll back, restore the pre-upgrade backup into a fresh database (the upgraded one has the newer schema) and start the image you noted, with the same key. Anything written after that backup is lost, so schedule upgrades when no import or agent work is running, and take the backup immediately before. Agent tokens carry over an upgrade. A token issued with a scope that a newer version retired is converted to its replacement during the upgrade, keeps working, and the conversion is recorded in the audit log. The authoritative spec for the encryption model is DESIGN.md section 9; see also Configuration for the key.

pages.title: Connect an agent
pages.description: Wire an MCP client to Purser with a scoped token and the right operating conventions.

sections.text: Purser's primary interface is its MCP server. Any MCP client that speaks streamable HTTP — Claude, an OpenClaw agent, a custom runtime — connects the same way.

sections.heading: Endpoint and auth
sections.text: - Endpoint: https://<purser-host /mcp (streamable HTTP, same process as REST) - Auth: Authorization: Bearer <api-token — the same scoped tokens REST uses Create the token in the admin UI ( Settings - Agents & API ) — the setup wizard also offers to mint one as its final step, with ready-to-paste config for the clients below. Recommended agent scopes: read + write . Scope Grants --- --- read Every read tool and resource write Every write, with your authority (audited and reversible) admin Token and configuration management (REST only) Your agent acts for you: with write it writes directly when carrying out your request, and proposes instead when acting on its own initiative (a draft rule or financial note, or a schedule suggestion). Every write is attributed to its token in the audit log and reversible. A token with only read + write cannot create tokens or grant itself more access. Token creation requires admin: reserve that scope for trusted administration.

sections.heading: First call: describe
sections.text: In every fresh session, call describe before anything else. One round-trip returns the data model, amount conventions, your token's scopes, the category tree, and the account list. The same guide is served unauthenticated at GET /llms.txt on the instance.

sections.heading: Operating conventions
sections.text: - Aggregate questions (spending, net worth, forecasts, unmatched) each have a dedicated tool — never page transactions and sum them in-context. - Amounts are decimal strings; negative means money out of the account. spending summary totals are positive-for-spend. - Accounts and categories accept a UUID or an ltree path like expenses.dining.coffee: dot-separated labels of letters, digits, and -. A malformed path comes back as an error naming the bad segment. - Bill emails: parse them agent-side and call create schedule or create transaction — Purser never parses email server-side. - trigger sync when the user asks for fresh data, not on every question — SimpleFIN Bridge allows 24 fetches per day. - Full series (forecast balance's daily uri, balance history's and net worth's series uri) are purser:// resources. A gateway or client that forwards tools but not resources reads them with the read series(uri) tool instead — same body, same auth, read scope.

sections.heading: Connect from your client
sections.text: Every client below wants the same two facts: the endpoint URL and the token. Substitute your host for purser.example.com throughout.

sections.heading: Claude (claude.ai and Claude Desktop)
sections.text: Open Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector and paste the server URL. Put the token under Request headers — header name Authorization, value Bearer <api-token (the whole value, including the word Bearer). The Request headers section is a beta feature still rolling out. If your account does not show it, the dialog only offers OAuth, which Purser does not implement yet — use Claude Code below, or any other client on this page.

sections.heading: Claude Code
sections.text: claude mcp add --transport http purser https://purser.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token "

sections.heading: Codex
sections.text: Codex (OpenAI's agent) shares one host config across the CLI, desktop app, and IDE extension: ~/.codex/config.toml (trusted projects can also use .codex/config.toml). The recommended form keeps the token out of the file by naming an environment variable: [mcp servers.purser] url = "https://purser.example.com/mcp" bearer token env var = "PURSER TOKEN" Export PURSER TOKEN where the Codex process can see it — GUI apps may not inherit your shell config. Restart the app or open a new thread so Codex rebuilds its tool list, then verify with codex mcp list. A literal http headers = { Authorization = "Bearer ..." } also works but stores the secret in plaintext config. ChatGPT web-chat connectors accept only OAuth or no authentication, so they cannot reach Purser yet — OAuth support is planned.

sections.heading: OpenClaw
