sections.text: openclaw mcp add purser --url https://purser.example.com/mcp \ --transport streamable-http \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token " Or directly in openclaw.json under mcp.servers, with the token supplied via environment variable: { "mcp": { "servers": { "purser": { "url": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "transport": "streamable-http", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${PURSER TOKEN}" } } } } } Restart the gateway afterwards so the tools are picked up.

sections.heading: Gemini CLI and Code Assist
sections.text: Both share ~/.gemini/settings.json, so one command covers both: gemini mcp add --transport http \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token " \ purser https://purser.example.com/mcp Or in settings.json (note httpUrl, not url, for streamable HTTP): { "mcpServers": { "purser": { "httpUrl": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${PURSER TOKEN}" } } } } The consumer Gemini app does not support custom MCP servers.

sections.heading: Any other MCP client
sections.text: { "mcpServers": { "purser": { "type": "http", "url": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <api-token " } } } } Clients that only speak stdio can bridge to the HTTP endpoint with mcp-remote. The full toolset is in the MCP tool catalog.

sections.heading: Replace a credential without splitting its audit history
sections.text: In Settings - Agents & API , choose Replace credential for ... under Integration identity when creating the replacement. The new credential keeps the same integration ID, with its own grant and effective permissions. Update the integrator to use it, then revoke the old credential. Creating a replacement does not automatically revoke the old one. Enable Show expired and revoked if you need to select an older credential. Only an administrator can create replacements, and they must belong to that administrator's user. Give separate integrations separate identities. A gateway credential shared by several agents identifies the gateway; Purser cannot infer which agent used it.

pages.title: Run with Docker Compose
pages.description: What the bundled compose files run, the .env file, the database password, remote access, the API and worker split, data, health checks and upgrades.

sections.text: Docker Compose is the supported way to run Purser. The Quickstart takes you from an empty directory to a running instance; this page explains what the compose files do and how to run them from then on.

sections.heading: What docker-compose.yml runs
sections.text: docker-compose.yml starts two containers on a private Compose network: Service What it does --- --- purser The published image for one release (ghcr.io/mlamoure/purser:v<version , linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). Its default command, purser serve, applies database migrations, starts the scheduled jobs (bank sync, matching and the other daily jobs) in the same process, then serves the web UI, the REST API and /mcp on port 8000. It runs with every Linux capability dropped and no-new-privileges, and restarts unless you stop it. postgres PostgreSQL 16. Its data lives in the named volume purser-pgdata. It is not published on any host port: only containers on the Compose network reach it. purser waits until postgres reports healthy before it starts. Purser keeps everything in that one database, so the volume is the whole instance, together with the encryption key, which is never stored in it.

sections.heading: The .env file
sections.text: Compose reads a file named .env in the same directory as docker-compose.yml and substitutes its values into the compose file. Keep it readable only by you (chmod 600 .env): it holds the encryption key. PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY=YOUR KEY POSTGRES PASSWORD=YOUR DATABASE PASSWORD PURSER PUBLIC URL=https://purser.example.com PURSER BIND ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 Variable Default Used for --- --- --- PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY none Required. Compose refuses to start without it. See Encryption at rest. POSTGRES PASSWORD purser The database password, given to both containers. See Set the database password. PURSER PUBLIC URL http://localhost:8000 The address people and agents use to reach Purser. PURSER BIND ADDRESS 127.0.0.1 The host interface the published port listens on. A Compose setting only; Purser itself never reads it. The .env file only fills in the compose file. docker-compose.yml passes the purser container its database URL, the encryption key and PURSER PUBLIC URL, and nothing else, so another line in .env (for example PURSER TIMEZONE) does not reach Purser. Set other variables in an override file (below), or set the runtime-editable ones in the admin UI under Settings .

sections.heading: Keep your changes in an override file
sections.text: Compose also reads docker-compose.override.yml from the same directory and merges it over docker-compose.yml. Put your own changes there rather than in docker-compose.yml, so that an upgrade can replace the release's file without losing them: docker-compose.override.yml services: purser: environment: PURSER TIMEZONE: America/New York Run docker compose config to see the merged result before you start it.

sections.heading: Set the database password
sections.text: The bundled database password defaults to purser. The database is reachable only from the Compose network, but change the default anyway, and do it before the first docker compose up : the PostgreSQL image sets the password only when it initialises an empty volume. Put a long random value of letters and digits in .env (the password is placed in a database URL, where characters such as @, :, / or would break it): echo "POSTGRES PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)" .env Once the volume exists, changing POSTGRES PASSWORD in .env alone does not change the database's password. Purser then fails to start, and its log shows password authentication failed for user "purser". To change it later, change it inside PostgreSQL first, then in .env: docker compose exec postgres psql -U purser -d purser At the purser= prompt, run \password purser, enter the new password twice, then \q. Put the same password in .env as POSTGRES PASSWORD and run docker compose up -d, which recreates both containers with the new value.

sections.heading: Reach Purser from other machines
sections.text: By default the published port listens on 127.0.0.1:8000, so only the Docker host itself can reach Purser. Finish the first-run setup (the admin account) before you open it to anything else: until the first admin exists, the setup page is open to whoever reaches it first. For access from other machines, put Purser behind an HTTPS reverse proxy and set PURSER PUBLIC URL to the HTTPS address; see Put Purser behind a reverse proxy. Only set PURSER BIND ADDRESS to another interface (for example a private LAN address) when something on that network needs to reach port 8000 directly, and never publish plain HTTP to the internet. PURSER PUBLIC URL must be the address people actually use: it decides whether the session cookie is marked secure, it is the base of the single sign-on redirect address, and the MCP endpoint refuses requests for any other host (HTTP 421). After changing it, run docker compose up -d.

sections.heading: Run the worker separately
sections.text: By default one purser container serves requests and also runs the scheduled jobs. docker-compose.split.yml moves the jobs into a second container from the same image: - the purser container gets PURSER DISABLE SCHEDULER=1 and only serves requests; - a new worker container runs purser worker, which runs only the scheduled jobs. It publishes no port and has no health check; read its state with docker compose logs worker. Download docker-compose.split.yml from the same release tag as docker-compose.yml, into the same directory, then name both files: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.split.yml up -d To avoid typing the file list every time, add it to .env: COMPOSE FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.split.yml:docker-compose.override.yml When you name files with -f or COMPOSE FILE, Compose no longer reads docker-compose.override.yml by itself, so list it too if you have one. Run exactly one worker . The jobs take no lock against each other, so a second worker would run every scheduled job again: each bank sync, matching run and webhook delivery pass would happen twice. Do not scale the worker service, and do not run a second copy of the stack against the same database.

sections.heading: Data and the named volume
sections.text: The database lives in the Docker volume purser-pgdata, which Compose names after the project, normally the directory name (for example purser purser-pgdata; docker volume ls shows it). - docker compose down removes the containers and keeps the volume. - docker compose down -v deletes the volume and every record in it. Back up with pg dump through the postgres container: umask 077 docker compose exec -T postgres pg dump -U purser --format=custom purser purser-backup.dump Backup and restore covers what a dump contains, the restore drill and key rotation.

sections.heading: Health checks
sections.text: Both containers have health checks, and docker compose ps shows their state: - purser requests GET /healthz inside the container every 30 seconds (after a 15 second start period) and is unhealthy after three failures. A healthy answer is {"status":"ok","database":"ok"}; it confirms the process is serving and the database answers, nothing more. - postgres runs pg isready every 10 seconds. Docker does not restart a container for being unhealthy; restart: unless-stopped restarts it when the process exits. Purser exits at startup when the key is missing or does not match the database, or when migrations fail, so a container that keeps restarting means you should read docker compose logs purser.

sections.heading: Upgrade
sections.text: Each release publishes its own compose files under its tag. To upgrade: 1. Take a backup, and keep the image tag you run now; there is no downgrade. Upgrade and roll back has the full procedure. 2. Download the new release's docker-compose.yml (and docker-compose.split.yml, if you use it) over the old one, keeping .env and docker-compose.override.yml. The download URL has the same form as in the Quickstart, with the new tag. 3. Pull and restart: docker compose pull docker compose up -d Migrations run automatically when the new container starts; with the split topology, the API and the worker take turns on a database lock, so they run once.

sections.text: - Quickstart: the first install. - Put Purser behind a reverse proxy: HTTPS for remote access. - Backup and restore: backups, restores, key rotation and upgrades. - Configuration: every PURSER variable. - Encryption at rest: what the key protects.

pages.title: Visualize with Grafana
pages.description: Point Grafana at Purser's stable read schema, import the shipped dashboards, and enable deep links on tool responses.

sections.text: Purser includes a forecast chart on the Scheduled transactions page and widgets for compatible MCP clients. Grafana provides broader reporting over a stable read schema, so your data remains available to dashboards outside the app. Three dashboards ship in the repository under grafana/dashboards/: - Purser - Monthly cash flow by category (purser-cash-flow) - Purser - Net worth over time (purser-net-worth) - Purser - Upcoming bills & forecast (purser-upcoming-bills)

sections.heading: The stable read schema
sections.text: The dashboards query a versioned readmodel schema — the query contract you can build your own panels against: View Feeds --- --- readmodel.v1 net worth daily Net worth, assets vs liabilities over time. readmodel.v1 spending by category month Cash flow by category and month. readmodel.v1 forecast daily Projected balances. readmodel.v1 holdings latest Latest brokerage holdings. readmodel.v2 transactions flat The flat transaction view. net worth daily is materialized and watermark-driven, so these read fast and stay current as new data lands.

sections.heading: Add a datasource and import
sections.text: 1. Create a read-only PostgreSQL role on the Purser database (the dashboards describe their input as a purser read connection). Reporting should never hold write access to the ledger. 2. In Grafana, add a PostgreSQL datasource pointing at the Purser database with that role. 3. Import each JSON file from grafana/dashboards/. On import Grafana prompts for the DS PURSER datasource input (labeled "Purser (PostgreSQL)") — select the datasource from step 2. The dashboards carry only grafana and postgres requirements, so no plugins are needed.

sections.heading: Deep links from tool responses
sections.text: Set PURSER GRAFANA URL to your Grafana base URL and Purser decorates tool responses with links.grafana deep links into the matching dashboard — so an agent's answer about net worth can offer the chart. When it is unset, links are omitted entirely. PURSER GRAFANA URL is runtime-editable in Settings - General ; see Configuration. The design rationale for a shared read schema, built-in visualizations and external dashboard templates is DESIGN.md principle 7 and section 8 (net worth).

pages.title: Track a house or other asset
pages.description: Keep the value of something you own and value by hand, such as a house or a car, as a ledger of changes, set its value on a date, and undo a wrong entry.

sections.text: A house, a car, land or jewelry has no bank feed that reports its value. In Purser such a thing is an account of type property (the app calls it an asset), and its value is a ledger like any other account: the sum of its entries. - A change in value is an entry. "The house went up 25,000.00 in June" is one posted transaction between the asset and the system account equity.revaluation. That account is not a category, so the change moves net worth and never shows up as spending or income. - A backdated change works like a backdated transaction. It moves every balance after it. - "Worth X on D" is a calculator. Reconcile the asset to a figure and Purser posts the difference as a change. - A wrong change is reversed, never edited, so the history keeps both.

sections.heading: Create the asset
sections.text: In the app, open Accounts and choose Add asset : a name, what it is (house, land, car, boat, RV, jewelry, art & collectibles, equipment or other), the purchase date and price, and an optional description such as an address or a VIN. The description is stored encrypted. The kind is a label and an icon only; it changes nothing about how the asset is valued, and it can be changed later. Over the API: curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/accounts" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name": "House", "type": "property", "path": "assets.house", "asset kind": "house", "acquired on": "2020-06-15"}' PATCH /accounts/{id} changes asset kind, acquired on and asset description later (an explicit null clears the date or the description). From an agent, update account takes asset kind.

sections.heading: Money put in
sections.text: What you paid for the asset is not a gain, so it is recorded as money put in : a value change with "kind": "capital", an entry against the system account equity.capital instead of equity.revaluation. The app's Add asset form records the purchase price this way. curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/accounts/$HOUSE ID/value-changes" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"as of": "2020-06-15", "amount": "450000.00", "kind": "capital", "note": "Purchase price"}' Use it for money no account in Purser paid: the purchase before your history starts, or an improvement paid in cash. When a tracked account paid (a new roof paid from checking), turn that payment into a transfer to the asset instead (in the register, choose the asset as the category, or update transaction with category="[assets.house]"). Either way it raises the asset's value without counting as a gain.

sections.heading: Record a change in value
sections.text: curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/accounts/$HOUSE ID/value-changes" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"as of": "2026-06-30", "amount": "25000.00", "note": "Appraisal"}' amount is signed: positive when the asset gained value, negative when it lost value. as of is today (in the household time zone) or earlier. The answer carries the entry's transaction id and the asset's balance now. reference makes a retry safe. Send the same reference again on the same asset and Purser posts nothing and answers 200 with the first change (created: false). A reference is stored in plaintext, so it takes letters, digits, ., , : and - only (for example valuation-2026-06); put words in note, which is stored encrypted. From an agent, the MCP tool record value change does the same (write scope).

sections.heading: Set the value on a date
sections.text: When you have a figure rather than a change (an appraisal, an estimate), reconcile the asset to it: curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/accounts/$HOUSE ID/reconcile" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"as of": "2026-11-01", "statement balance": "612500.00", "note": "Estimate midpoint"}' Purser compares the figure with the asset's value on that date and posts the difference against equity.revaluation (category in the answer), dated as of. It follows the reconciliation rules: - One value per date. Sending the same figure for a recorded date again answers created: false and posts nothing, which makes a scheduled job safe to retry. A different figure for that date is 409 reconciliation conflict. - Only forward. A date before the asset's latest recorded value is 409 reconciliation out of order. To change history, record a backdated change instead. - Never stale silently. A later backdated change, or a reversal, moves the value on a recorded date. That value then reads out of balance, with the difference, on GET /accounts/{id}/reconciliations and in list accounts. From an agent, use reconcile account with the value as statement balance.

sections.heading: Undo a wrong change
sections.text: curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/value-changes/$TRANSACTION ID/reverse" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" This works for a change recorded directly and for one a reconcile posted. Purser corrects it through a reversal pair, so the original stays in the history next to the reversal. The answer's amount is what was taken back. Editing the row with PATCH /transactions/{id} is refused. From an agent, use reverse value change.

sections.heading: Get reminded to update a value
sections.text: Give an asset revalue after days (on creation, PATCH /accounts/{id}, the app's Edit details , or update account(revalue after days=...) from an agent; null, or 0 from an agent, turns it off). When the asset's value was last stated longer ago than that, Purser: - marks it stale: true on the account (asset.last valued says when), - emits asset.stale once, from the daily check at 07:20 UTC, - and lists it in whats new under stale assets until a value is recorded. Any live value entry counts as stating the value, and so does a recorded value on a date even when it matched and posted nothing. A monthly estimate that did not move still refreshes the asset. A reversed entry does not count.

sections.heading: Equity and the loans an asset secures
sections.text: Point a loan at the asset that secures it (a mortgage at its house, a car loan at its car) and the asset reports its equity : its value plus the loans' balances, which are negative while owed. curl -s -X PATCH "$PURSER URL/accounts/$MORTGAGE ID" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"secured by id\": \"$HOUSE ID\"}" The asset then carries equity and secured loan ids on GET /accounts (with balances) and GET /accounts/{id}; the loan carries secured by id. An explicit null unlinks it. In the app, the asset's page lists its loans with Link a loan and Unlink . From an agent, update account takes secured by (the asset's path, or "" to clear it), and list accounts shows asset kind, equity, secured loans and secured by.

sections.heading: Money put in and gain
sections.text: Every asset reports two figures that add up to its value: money put in (the purchase and every transfer in or out) and gain (the sum of its changes in value; negative is a loss). They are on the account (asset.money put in, asset.gain), in list accounts, and on the asset's page. They are ledger sums, not a tax calculation.

sections.heading: Sell or dispose of an asset
sections.text: 1. Record the sale's money as transfers out of the asset, dated on or before the sale: the bank's deposit of the proceeds (in that account's register, choose the asset as the category) and any loan payoff made at closing. 2. Then dispose of it, in the app with Sell or dispose… on the asset's page, or: curl -s -X POST "$PURSER URL/accounts/$HOUSE ID/dispose" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"as of": "2027-06-30", "note": "Sold", "dry run": true}' Whatever is left on the asset on that date is the rest of its change in value (selling costs included): a gain or a loss, or, when no proceeds were recorded, its whole value (a write-off, such as a car that was totalled). Purser posts it against equity.revaluation on the sale date and closes the account at zero, so net worth drops on the sale date even when you record it weeks later, and nothing lands in a spending category. value before, closing change and the total gain come back; run it with dry run first. A sale dated before the asset's latest entry is refused. From an agent, use dispose asset. Closing an asset with Close… (or POST /accounts/{id}/close) does the same, dated today.

sections.heading: Where the value shows
sections.text: - The asset's balance on every surface is its postings sum (balance method: "postings"), the same as a checking account's. - Net worth adds it like any other account. - In the app, the asset's page shows its kind, equity, Record value (a value on a date) and Change value (a change, or money put in), and every entry in the register below with Undo . - In the register, its entries carry value change: true (and money put in: true for money put in). In review batch they are flagged value change: mark one reviewed when the figure is right, reverse it when it is not. Each change emits an asset.value changed event (see Events and webhooks).

sections.heading: An asset with a bank feed
sections.text: A few feeds report the value of an account mapped as property. After each sync, when the reported balance differs from the asset's balance on that day, Purser posts a value change for the difference (origin import, note "Balance the bank reported"). Such an asset is never part of the balance-drift check.

sections.heading: Loans are different
sections.text: A loan's balance is still its latest valuation (record valuation), because a mortgage feed reports a balance and nothing else. See Recording a valuation.

pages.title: Import QIF and CSV
pages.description: Load bank history from a Quicken QIF or CSV export with a mapping-first preview, per-account cutoffs, and content-hash idempotency.

sections.text: When an account has no SimpleFIN feed, or you want history older than the feed reaches, import a file your bank exports. Purser reads Quicken QIF and two CSV layouts through POST /import/qif and POST /import/csv — a two-step preview then commit , sharing one planner so every rule below applies identically to QIF and CSV.

sections.heading: Preview, then commit
sections.text: The preview is a strict, read-only dry run: it resolves your account mapping, suggests a cutoff and a sign per account, and returns the real counts it gets by checking content hashes against the database. Its per-account numbers equal what the commit will do for the same request — an exact rehearsal where only the commit writes rows. Adjust mapping, cutoff, and invert, then commit the identical request.

sections.heading: Mapping first
sections.text: Every file account maps to one Purser account. The preview drives the account selector (or inline account creation); a single-account file uses the parser's default name. For a multi-account CSV you can import a subset: set a file account's map value to null to skip it. Its rows are removed before planning and counted skipped unmapped, and any transfer whose counterpart was skipped degrades to a one-leg entry on the imported side. Per-account skip is a CSV surface (QIF's request map is not nullable), with one QIF exception: an investment account (next section) may simply be left out of the map.

sections.heading: Investment accounts
sections.text: Purser imports bank registers, not investment activity. A QIF file's !Type:Invst sections (buys, sells, dividends, share moves, and the investment side of transfers) are skipped and counted skipped investment in the preview and the commit, and the preview lists the account as brokerage. An investment account you leave unmapped stays out entirely: a checking transfer into it imports as a one-leg entry on the checking side, so the checking balance matches Quicken's. Map it only if you want those transfers as two-leg transfers into a Purser account; it then receives the transfers, never the purchases. A brokerage balance adds the holdings' market value to its postings (see the three methods), so importing the purchases as well would count every contribution twice. The investment section never books a transfer of its own, so a contribution no longer reaches checking twice either.

sections.heading: Cutoffs: manual owns the past, the feed owns the present
sections.text: Each mapped account may carry a cutoff date. A row imports only when its date is strictly older than the cutoff — the feed owns everything from the cutoff forward, so manual history and SimpleFIN never fight over the same days. The server never imposes a cutoff you did not send ; the preview only suggests one: the account's earliest feed-sourced transaction date minus a 3-day margin (QIF carries transaction dates, while SimpleFIN posted dates run 1-3 business days later), or null when the feed has not touched the account. This is the per-request twin of the persistent feed start boundary.

sections.heading: Sign invert
sections.text: Some banks export a card or loan file with spending as a positive number. A per-account invert flips every row's amount before hashing, category selection, payee memory, and transfer direction. The preview computes a sign diagnostic and pre-checks invert when a credit-card or loan target looks income-positive. Footgun: re-importing the same file with invert toggled produces a disjoint set of content hashes and therefore duplicates. The preview's skipped dedup count stays 0 across such a flip, which is the tell — watch it.

sections.heading: Transfers and the bracket convention
sections.text: A row whose category is another account in Quicken brackets ([assets.savings]) is a transfer, evaluated against both accounts' effective cutoffs: - older than both cutoffs - the two-leg transfer; - inside both - skipped (skipped cutoff), the feed owns that window; - split (older than one side, inside the other) - degrades to a one-leg flat entry on the older side, which the post-import auto-link pass then pairs with the feed counterpart (see Transfers). Zero-amount marker rows are structurally non-importable (the ledger rejects zero postings), so the planner filters them into skipped zero amount before hashing -- a $0 Quicken row can never fail a commit or half-form a transfer.

sections.heading: Split transactions
sections.text: A Quicken row can be split across several categories (S, E and $ lines; its category reads --Split--). Purser imports it as one split transaction: one leg on the bank account and one leg per category line, so a paycheck's gross pay and taxes, or a store run that was half groceries, land in their own categories. - A transfer line (S[Savings]) is taken out of the split and imported as an ordinary transfer to that account, which pairs with the savings account's own copy of the row in the same file. The money moves once, and the checking balance matches Quicken's. The preview counts these lines split transfers; they follow every transfer rule above, cutoffs included. - A line with no category goes to the uncategorized placeholder, never to the payee's usual category. If the lines do not add up to the row's amount, the difference goes there too, counted split remainders. - A split left with a single category line imports as an ordinary row. Split rows are read-only: they cannot be recategorized or edited in place, and neither the categorize pass nor a rule's apply-history touches them. A file imported before split lines were read landed each split row whole under expenses.split; importing it again dedups against those rows, so to get the lines, purge that import's batch first (purser admin purge-retired-rows, see the CLI reference) and import again.

sections.heading: CSV specifics
sections.text: /import/csv auto-detects two layouts by header row: an Amex activity export (Date, Description, Amount) of flat rows into a single account, and a Quicken CSV export (Date, Payee, Amount[, Category, Memo, Account, Clr, Scheduled]) where an Account column groups file accounts, a bracket Category is a transfer, and the Clr (or Cleared) and Scheduled columns drive the rules in the next section. When neither header matches, supply an explicit column map (date, amount and payee, plus optional memo, category, account, cleared and scheduled); until then the preview returns 422 csv layout unrecognized with the detected columns so a UI can offer a mapping form. Amounts are parsed as Decimal only (accountant negatives like (1,234.56) are read; float-looking garbage is a clear 422). CSV has no opening-balance convention, so mind any offset against a known statement balance.

sections.heading: Reminders and the cleared flag
sections.text: Quicken can include reminder rows in a CSV export: upcoming bills and deposits its register shows ahead of time, flagged in a Scheduled column. They are not history. The planner skips them, counts them skipped scheduled in both the preview and the commit, and never creates a row for them — model a recurring bill as a schedule instead. The file's cleared flag decides each remaining row's status: - QIF reads the C field: or c is cleared, X or R reconciled, and no C means uncleared. CSV reads the Clr or Cleared column, ignoring case: c, R, , X, Y, or the words cleared, reconciled, yes or true mark a cleared row; blank, N, U, or the words uncleared, no or false mean uncleared. Any other value is a 422, never a guess. - The flag counts per file account . In an account that marks at least one row cleared, an unmarked row is uncleared. An account with no marks at all — any bank-generated export, or a Quicken cash account nobody reconciles — carries no clearing information, so all of its rows count as cleared and import exactly as they always did. The same goes for a CSV with no cleared column. - Cleared rows land posted. Uncleared rows land expected and are counted uncleared: the bank has not seen them yet (an uncashed check), so they stay out of the balance — which keeps the balance-drift check comparing like with like — appear in the forecast (an overdue one lands today), raise bill.late like any unmatched expectation, and are settled by the matcher when the bank's posted row arrives. They never land pending: a feed sync voids any imported pending row it no longer lists, wherever that row came from. - A transfer lands expected only when no leg in the file is cleared; once either bank has seen it, it posts. A split transfer's one-leg entry follows its own leg, and opening balances always post. The preview's counts show both numbers before you commit, and the import page spells them out. When a later export marks a row cleared that an earlier import left expected, the commit posts that row in place instead of adding another, and the preview and the result count it promoted (once per leg for a transfer, which promotes when any of its legs is now marked). Only a mark promotes: an account with no marks carries no clearing information, and neither does a CSV without a cleared column. Promotion is limited to accounts without a feed — on a feed-connected account the matcher settles the row against the bank's posted row when it arrives, and posting it from the file as well would count that charge twice. Schedule instances and feed rows are never touched. Anything still expected can be posted by hand (POST /transactions/{id}/post) or voided.

sections.heading: Idempotency
sections.text: Both formats are content-hash idempotent over a shared qif: namespace. Re-run any import, or interleave manual imports with SimpleFIN syncs on one account, and you get zero new rows — the same history in either format dedups, expected rows included, and a reminder stays skipped. Identical rows are not duplicates. Two coffees on the same day at the same price are two rows in the file and two in the ledger: the second identical row in a file is the second occurrence of that content, an identity of its own. The count restarts in every file, so re-importing the file — or a later export that overlaps it — lands on the same identities and adds nothing. The same holds for transfers: two identical same-day transfers are two transfers, and so is a same-day round trip between two accounts. If an older import left only one row for such a pair, the next file that carries the pair adds the missing one, once. Both formats are raw-first: the verbatim upload is archived to raw fetches before any ledger write, and re-uploading an identical file archives nothing new. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 7.2.

pages.title: Deploy on Kubernetes with Helm
pages.description: Experimental. Install the Helm chart against an external Postgres with the encryption key in a Secret, review its locked-down defaults, and optionally split the worker role.

sections.text: Experimental: outside the supported release matrix. The Helm chart is kept and its defaults are hardened, but it has not been qualified against a real cluster , and releases are not tested on it. Docker Compose, in the Quickstart, is the supported deployment. Expect rough edges here. The chart lives in the repository at charts/purser. Its default image is the published ghcr.io/mlamoure/purser, tagged v + the chart's appVersion (for example v2026.10.0); to run your own build, push it to your registry and set image.repository. It runs the same one-image, multi-role design as every other deployment: an api Deployment (purser serve) and an optional worker.

sections.heading: Install
sections.text: The chart ships no encryption key, database URL or password, and refuses to render without them. Put them in a Secret first. The Secret must carry PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY and PURSER DATABASE URL; every other key in it also reaches the pods as an environment variable, so OIDC or AI-provider secrets can live there too. kubectl create secret generic purser-secrets \ --from-literal=PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY="$(python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate key().decode())')" \ --from-literal=PURSER DATABASE URL='postgresql+psycopg://purser:CHANGE ME@db.example.com:5432/purser' helm install purser charts/purser --set existingSecret=purser-secrets Record the encryption key somewhere safe (read it back with kubectl get secret purser-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data.PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY}' base64 -d): encrypted data is unrecoverable without it. purser keygen prints a key too. Instead of existingSecret you can pass secrets.encryptionKey and secrets.databaseUrl (plus secrets.extra for further secret variables), and the chart creates the Secret. Those values then live in your Helm release history, so prefer an existing Secret. Then port-forward to reach the first-run wizard, and connect agents to /mcp with a Bearer token exactly as elsewhere: kubectl port-forward svc/purser 8000:8000

sections.heading: Postgres: external or bundled
sections.text: postgres.mode chooses the database: - external (default): bring your own database through the Secret's PURSER DATABASE URL. It needs the ltree and pgcrypto extensions. For CloudNativePG, point the URL at the cluster's read-write service, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://purser:CHANGE ME@purser-rw:5432/purser. - bundled : a single-replica Postgres StatefulSet in the release, for evaluation only. It has no backups. Set postgres.password (16 or more characters of letters, digits and . ~ -; openssl rand -hex 24 gives one) or postgres.existingSecret. The chart keeps the password in its own Secret, and derives the app's database URL from it when you do not set one.

sections.heading: Secure defaults
sections.text: Every pod runs as the image's unprivileged user (UID and GID 999) with runAsNonRoot, a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, every Linux capability dropped and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. /tmp is a size-limited emptyDir; Purser writes nothing else to disk. No service-account token is mounted, because Purser never calls the Kubernetes API. The chart refuses to render when: - the encryption key or the database URL is missing; - a secret-shaped variable (one whose name contains SECRET, PASSWORD, TOKEN or API KEY, the encryption key or the database URL) is set under env, which renders as plain text in the pod spec: use secrets.extra or your Secret; - more than one scheduler would run (see the worker split below); - image.digest is not a sha256: digest. Value Default Notes --- --- --- image.repository ghcr.io/mlamoure/purser The published image. image.tag empty: v + the chart's appVersion The release tag format. image.digest empty sha256:... pins the exact image. image.pullPolicy IfNotPresent existingSecret empty Recommended. Needs PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY and PURSER DATABASE URL. secrets.encryptionKey, secrets.databaseUrl empty Required when existingSecret is not set. secrets.extra empty Further secret variables for the chart's Secret. env PURSER LOG LEVEL: INFO Plain settings for both roles. postgres.mode external bundled for evaluation only. postgres.password empty Bundled mode only; no default. api.replicas 1 Above 1 only with the worker enabled. api.resources requests 100m CPU, 256Mi; limits 1 CPU, 1Gi An idle API holds about 155 MiB. worker.enabled false worker.resources requests 50m CPU, 192Mi; limits 1 CPU, 1Gi An idle worker holds about 95 MiB. service.type ClusterIP ingress.enabled false networkPolicy.enabled false Ingress rules for the API and the bundled database. serviceAccount.automountToken false podSecurityContext, containerSecurityContext locked down as above Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES), which bounds the memory an import can take.

sections.heading: Probes and migrations
sections.text: Every role applies database migrations when it starts, before the API listens. The startup probe calls /healthz and allows five minutes by default (api.startupProbe), so long migrations are not killed. Readiness also uses /healthz, which answers 200 only while the database answers, so a database outage takes the pod out of the Service. Liveness checks only that the server accepts connections, so a database outage does not restart the pod.

sections.heading: Optional worker split
sections.text: By default the API process also runs the scheduler. To split jobs onto a dedicated worker (same image, purser worker), enable it: helm upgrade purser charts/purser --reuse-values --set worker.enabled=true The chart then sets PURSER DISABLE SCHEDULER=true on the API pods, so only the worker runs jobs. Exactly one scheduler ever runs: the chart pins the worker to one replica, refuses api.replicas above 1 while there is no worker, and uses the Recreate strategy for whichever Deployment runs the scheduler, so an old and a new pod never overlap during a rollout. Both roles apply database migrations when they start. They take turns on a Postgres advisory lock, so pods starting together are safe: the second waits for the first, then finds the schema already current.

sections.heading: Ingress and TLS
sections.text: The ingress is off by default, and the Service is a ClusterIP on port 8000. ingress.enabled=true (with ingress.host, className, tls and annotations) exposes it. Set ingress.tls to a Secret holding the certificate, or terminate TLS in front of the ingress: ingress: enabled: true className: nginx host: purser.example.com tls: - secretName: purser-tls hosts: [purser.example.com] With an ingress, the chart sets PURSER PUBLIC URL to https:// plus ingress.host. That URL drives secure cookies, the OIDC redirect URI, and the host allowlist of the MCP endpoint, which rejects requests for any other host (HTTP 421). Set env.PURSER PUBLIC URL yourself when users reach Purser at another URL or through something other than this ingress. App settings go under env, which feeds both Deployments; a variable you set there always replaces the value the chart would derive. Every PURSER variable is documented in Configuration. Behind an ingress, every request reaches the pod from the ingress controller, so set env.FORWARDED ALLOW IPS (uvicorn's trusted-proxy list) to the controller's pod network. Otherwise sign-in throttling counts every client as one address. Throttle counts live in each pod: with api.replicas above 1, each replica keeps its own.

sections.heading: Network policy
sections.text: networkPolicy.enabled=true limits ingress to the API port to the peers in networkPolicy.apiIngressFrom (by default, pods in the release's namespace; add your ingress controller's namespace), refuses all ingress to the worker, and lets only this release's Purser pods reach the bundled database. Egress is not restricted: Purser calls your bank feed, OIDC provider, AI provider and webhook targets. The authoritative deployment topology is DESIGN.md section 2.

pages.title: Track tax lots and equity awards
pages.description: Load a broker's lot list and award schedule into a hand-tracked position, record lot-aware sales and vests, and correct mistakes, through the REST API or MCP.

sections.text: A position you track by hand can also track its tax lots : when each block of shares was acquired, how many remain, and what they cost. An account can also hold equity awards (grants with a vest schedule). Purser stores and checks this data and serves it back. Reading it off a broker's site is your job or your agent's: Purser has no broker logins, no scraping and no scheduling of its own. Lots and awards are a sub-ledger: - The share count is still the history of the position's events, so prices, balances and net worth work exactly as before. - A position that tracks lots reports its lots' basis as its cost basis. The basis is null while any share sits in a lot with no basis or outside every lot. It is never an average. - Unvested award units are never counted in net worth, balances or holdings. The design and every rule are in DESIGN.md section 8 (decision 107).

sections.heading: Load a broker's lot list
sections.text: A capture is one observation of the broker's lots as of a day. Send every lot row the broker shows for a symbol, with the shares remaining in it: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/accounts/<account-id /lot-captures \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "as of": "2026-11-14", "captured at": "2026-11-14T15:02:00Z", "completeness": "complete", "source note": "broker holdings page", "positions": [{ "symbol": "ACME", "lots": [ {"external ref": "L-1001", "acquired on": "2024-02-05", "quantity": "12.5", "basis per share": "101.250000", "plan": "Monthly purchase", "acquisition": "plan purchase"}, {"external ref": "L-1002", "acquired on": "2025-08-05", "quantity": "3", "plan": "Matching award", "acquisition": "rsu vest"} ] }] }' - A dry run is the default. The answer is the plan: changes such as new lot, recount, fill basis and assign ref, any conflicts, and a plan hash. Nothing is written. - To apply , send the same body again with "dry run": false and "expect hash": "<plan hash ". If anything changed in between, the answer is 409 with preview stale and a fresh plan hash. Review the plan again before you commit. - Retries are safe. The exact same request again (the same captured at, as of, note and rows) writes nothing and returns the first capture (retry: true). The same holdings read again later, with a new captured at, records a new capture for freshness (repeat of) and changes nothing else. - Identity. A row matches a lot by external ref, the broker's lot reference, when it shows one. Otherwise it matches by acquisition date, plan and ordinal. Rows of one date and plan without a reference need distinct ordinals, kept in a stable order between captures. Several lots from the same vest stay separate. - Basis. Give basis per share, cost basis (the total for the remaining shares), or both if they agree. A total you give is kept exactly as given. Leave both out when the basis is unknown: it stays unknown and is never stored as 0. A row with no shares left carries no basis. - complete or partial. A complete capture lists the broker's whole list for each symbol it names. Purser then recounts the position up to the broker's total, because new lots explain the extra shares. A partial capture changes only the rows it lists and never changes the share count. Symbols a capture does not name are left alone. Over MCP the same contract is upsert lots(account, as of, captured at, completeness, positions, dry run=true). Then commit with dry run=false, expect hash=.... captured at is required: a commit must repeat the request exactly.

sections.heading: What becomes a conflict
sections.text: Purser never infers a sale, a deletion or an edit from a capture. When a capture shows something the book cannot explain, it is a conflict, and nothing is applied for that symbol: Conflict Meaning Resolve it by --- --- --- quantity decrease A lot has fewer shares than Purser holds for it Recording the sale (or transfer out) that drew on it, naming the lot, then capturing again quantity increase A lot has more shares Reversing the wrong disposal, or voiding the lot and capturing again missing from capture A complete capture leaves out a lot that still holds shares Recording what took it, or voiding it if it was wrong unexplained decrease A complete total is below Purser's count, with every lot accounted for Recording the disposal first basis differs The broker's basis differs Capturing again with basis policy: "replace" basis locked The basis differs, and a disposal already drew on the lot Reversing the disposal, correcting the basis, recording the disposal again insufficient unallocated A partial capture's new lots need more shares than sit outside lots Using a complete capture, or recording the shares first ambiguous identity / identity mismatch Rows and lots cannot be told apart, or a reference names a lot of another date or plan Adding references or ordinals stale capture The capture is older than one already applied: an earlier as of, or the same day read at an earlier captured at Nothing: it is compared, never applied skip conflicts: true applies the symbols that have no conflicts. It skips the others whole and still records the capture as evidence.

sections.heading: Sell or move shares from lots
sections.text: On a day a position's lots can be drawn on, a sell or transfer out must name the lots it takes. Without them it is refused with allocation required. curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/positions/<position-id /events \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"kind": "sell", "occurred on": "2026-11-14", "quantity": "5", "price": "150", "lots": [{"external ref": "L-1001", "quantity": "5"}]}' - Specific identification: lots: [{lot id external ref, quantity}]. {"unallocated": true, "quantity": ...} takes shares that sit outside every lot. Use the broker's own lot choice when it shows one. - A method: lot method is one of: - fifo: oldest acquisition first. - lifo: newest first. - hifo: highest basis per share first. It is refused while a candidate lot has no basis. A method never takes unallocated shares. - Cash. A sale's cash works exactly as on any hand-tracked position: the double-count check, transaction id links and settle on all apply. - What is recorded. Each disposition records its basis, its share of the net proceeds, the realized gain when both are known, and the term. A disposal is long only after the one-year anniversary of the acquisition. - Basis is conserved exactly. The disposal that empties a lot takes the remaining basis. A sale's proceeds are split across its lots exactly, and no lot gets a share of the other sign. - transfer out records shares that left with no price and no cash, such as a move to another broker. It is never a sale. Over MCP: record sale(..., lots=[{lot, quantity}]) or record sale(..., lot method="fifo"), and record transfer out. A buy on a lot-tracked position opens its own lot. Pass "unallocated": true to keep the shares outside every lot.

sections.heading: Load awards and record vests
sections.text: An award capture lists each grant (grant ref, symbol, granted on, granted quantity, cancelled quantity, the broker's vested quantity) and the vests still to come (schedule: [{vest date, quantity}]). Send it to POST /accounts/{id}/award-captures, or over MCP to upsert awards. It follows the same dry-run, expect hash, retry and conflict contract as a lot capture. Purser applies these changes: - new grants and new vests - a re-estimated scheduled quantity - more cancelled units - a new reported vested count These are conflicts, never applied: - a changed grant size - fewer cancelled units - a scheduled future vest that a complete capture no longer lists. Purser never forfeits it by itself; forfeit it explicitly with PATCH /award-vests/{id} (MCP update award vest). Purser works out each award's units from all the evidence: - Vested: the broker's reported vested count, plus the vests you recorded after its date. Purser keeps that count when a later capture leaves it out. Vests you recorded on or before its date are already in it, so they are never counted twice. - Cancelled: the larger of the broker's cancelled count and the units of vests you marked forfeited. Both describe units that will never vest, so a forfeiture the broker also reports as cancelled is counted once. - Unvested: granted minus cancelled minus vested. It is split into scheduled units (dated vests still to come) and unscheduled units (no vest date yet). - Unknown: if the broker never reported a vested count and the recorded vests and schedule don't account for every unit, Purser reports only the scheduled units and marks the total as not known (unvested known: false, complete: false). - Limits: a capture, a vest, reinstating a vest, or correcting granted or cancelled units is refused if vested, scheduled and cancelled units would add up to more than the grant. When a vest happens, record it: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/awards/<award-id /vests \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"vest date": "2026-11-05", "gross quantity": "10", "withheld quantity": "3.5", "fmv": "60"}' - By default a vest event adds the net shares (gross minus withheld) and opens their lot, with the fair market value as its basis. - All units withheld (withheld quantity equal to gross quantity): the vest is recorded with no shares and no lot. - If you already captured the broker's lot list, the vest's lot is already there. Pass "lot": "<lot id or reference " to link it instead: no shares are added. The lot must meet all of these: - on the award's account and symbol - acquired on the vest date - holding the net shares, or fewer if some were sold before the capture - with the fair market value as its basis - Duplicates are refused. Purser refuses the vest as a possible duplicate when an unlinked lot acquired that day exists and neither lot nor force new lot was given. A vest is never counted twice. - Retries are safe. The same vest again with the same figures is a no-op (already recorded). Different figures are a 409 vest conflict. Unvested units appear in these places, always outside net worth: - GET /accounts/{id}/awards and MCP list awards: the units per symbol, their value at the latest close, and the next vest. - MCP list holdings: an unvested block per account (the three largest symbols; unvested more counts the rest). list awards answers a page at a time: the awards, or with award one award's vest schedule, continue with next cursor. The per-symbol summary comes on the first page.

sections.heading: Read it back
sections.text: - Lots: GET /positions/{id}/lots (MCP list lots) returns the lots in FIFO order, a page at a time. Its summary gives: - the shares in lots, and the shares outside every lot (unallocated) - the shares in lots with no basis - the lots' total basis - capture: when the broker's lots were last captured The price's own date, price as of on the position, is a different kind of freshness. - One lot: GET /lots/{id} returns a lot and every disposition that drew on it. A disposition shows live: false once its event is reversed. - Realized gains: GET /accounts/{id}/realized-gains?year=2026 (MCP realized gains) gives totals by term. Shares without a basis or proceeds are counted, never valued as 0. Purser computes no tax. - Captures: GET /accounts/{id}/captures lists the account's captures, newest first.

sections.heading: Correct a mistake
sections.text: Every correction is audited. Events are corrected by reversal; lot-basis corrections update the lot and retain the previous and new basis in the audit log: - A lot opened by an event (a buy or a vest) goes when you reverse that event: POST /position-events/{id}/reverse, MCP reverse position event. The lot shows as reversed, and its reference is free, so you can record the corrected buy or vest with the same reference. The reversal is refused while a disposal still draws on the lot: reverse the disposal first. - A lot adopted from a capture is voided with POST /lots/{id}/void (MCP void lot). Then capture again with a new captured at to record the right lot. The void is refused while a disposal draws on the lot or a vest is linked to it. - A wrong basis is corrected with PATCH /lots/{id} (MCP correct lot basis), only while no disposal has drawn on the lot. Otherwise reverse the disposals, correct the basis, and record them again. - A vest linked to the wrong lot , or one recorded with every unit withheld, goes back to scheduled with PATCH /award-vests/{id} ("status": "scheduled").

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Lot references and grant ids are account identifiers. They are encrypted at rest. Agents never see them unless a call asks with include: ["external ids"], and REST omits them for non-admin API tokens. You can always pass a reference to name a lot or an award. Plan labels follow the purchase-privacy setting. A lot's basis (its per-share figure too), proceeds and gains follow the amount-privacy setting. Realized-gain totals are aggregates.

sections.heading: Not covered
sections.text: These are out of scope: - tax forms and tax computation - ESPP qualifying flags - splits and other corporate actions - importing a CSV lot export - vest events in the forecast For record vest and POST /awards/{id}/vests, withheld quantity is required. Supply explicit zero only when the evidence confirms nothing was withheld. Sold or withdrawn shares do not establish tax withholding. If the historical withholding is unknown, keep the owned lot and award baseline and leave that vest event unrecorded until evidence is available. Importing lots does not correct cash. For a manual brokerage account, use cash reconciliation with component: "cash", excluding both securities and unvested awards from the cash target.

pages.title: Docker on macOS
pages.description: Run Purser in Linux containers on macOS; the published arm64 image is verified on Apple Silicon.

sections.text: Purser uses Docker Compose on macOS. There is no supported native macOS installer, Homebrew database installation, or Purser LaunchAgent.

sections.heading: Apple Silicon status
sections.text: Docker Desktop and Colima on Apple Silicon run Linux arm64 containers. Purser is built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, each natively on its own architecture, and Compose pulls the arm64 image on an Apple Silicon Mac. The published image is verified there: on 2026-10-28 it passed the release's end-to-end drills (onboarding, backup and restore, upgrade, crash and outage recovery, and failure journeys) on an Apple M1 with Colima and Docker, running natively with no emulation. Follow Set up Purser with your AI or the Quickstart. Docker runs both Purser and PostgreSQL. You do not need host Python, Node or Git. Keep the encryption key separately from database backups and retain the PostgreSQL named volume when recreating containers.

sections.heading: Restart and recovery
sections.text: Compose restarts containers while the Docker engine is running. Configure your Docker runtime to start when you log in if you want Purser available after a Mac restart. Purser does not install a macOS login agent. Use Backup and restore before upgrades. Never remove the database volume as a troubleshooting step without a verified backup. Purser is not published on PyPI. Do not install an unrelated package by the bare name purser.

pages.title: Track holdings by hand
pages.description: Record what a brokerage account holds when its feed sends cash but no holdings, keep those positions priced, and see how they reach balances and net worth.

sections.text: Some brokerages send an account's cash through SimpleFIN but no holdings. An employee stock plan is the usual case: the shares sit at the broker, the feed shows only the cash that leaves. Without holdings, the account reports its cash alone and net worth leaves the shares out. Purser can track such an account's holdings by hand. You (or your agent) record what the account holds, Purser prices it every day, and the value reaches the account's balance and net worth exactly like a feed snapshot would.

sections.heading: Switch the account to manual holdings
sections.text: An account's holdings come from one source at a time: the feed (the default) or positions recorded by hand. An admin switches a brokerage account, once: curl -X PATCH https://purser.example.com/accounts/<id \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"holdings source": "manual"}' In the admin UI the switch is the Holdings selector on the account page (admins only). - The feed keeps importing the account's cash transactions. It stops recording holdings for it: those rows are counted as holdings skipped manual in the sync result, and they stay in the archived fetch. - Feed snapshots recorded before the switch stay as history. The first hand-tracked snapshot is dated the day after the last feed one, so no date mixes the two sources. - Switching back to feed needs the account to be mapped to a feed account (a 422 otherwise) and changes no snapshot: the hand-tracked holdings stay in effect, so the account keeps its value, until the first sync after the switch ends the hand-tracked period. From that sync's date the account holds what the feed reports, and a position the feed does not report ends there (all of them, for a feed that sends only cash). The sync result counts what it ended (manual period tombstones), and the audit log records it as account.manual period end. The hand-tracked history before stays, and so do your positions and their events, read-only, until the account is switched to manual again. Unmapping or closing the account before that sync ends the period the same day; remapping it onto another feed account does not (that mapping's first sync ends it). If no sync of the account arrives for the price staleness threshold (7 days by default), the daily price job reports it once (holding.period open, and a whats new line): the hand-tracked holdings are still counted, unpriced by anything new, so check the connection or the account's mapping. Only brokerage accounts take a holdings source.

sections.heading: Record what the account holds
sections.text: "I hold 412.5 shares of ACME as of 2026-10-14" is one call. From an agent: record position(account="assets.plan", symbol="ACME", quantity="412.5", as of="2026-10-14", source note="broker holdings page, 2026-10-14") Over REST, open the position with its opening quantity: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/accounts/<id /positions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"symbol": "ACME", "quantity": "412.5", "as of": "2026-10-14"}' In the admin UI, the account page gains a Positions tab with + position and a Set quantity editor on every row. - quantity is a decimal string, up to 6 places. cost basis (optional) is the TOTAL basis of that quantity; with it, positions report an unrealized gain. Left out, a re-count of the same number of shares keeps the basis, a changed count makes it unknown, and zero shares have a basis of zero. The Set quantity editor sends a basis only when you type one; the field shows the current basis as a hint. - as of is today or earlier. A backdated quantity re-values history from that date, and net worth heals by itself. - Writes need write scope. A position has no draft state: a record is final, and a correction is a new event.

sections.heading: Buys, sells and corrections
sections.text: A position's history is a list of events: Event Means --- --- set quantity The account holds exactly this many shares on that date. buy It gained this many shares; with a price, the cost basis grows by quantity × price + fees. With funded from: "cash" its cost also leaves the account's cash (below). sell It lost this many shares; the basis drops at average cost. Its proceeds land on the account's cash unless proceeds to is "none" (below). curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/positions/<position id /events \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"kind": "sell", "occurred on": "2026-10-01", "quantity": "20", "price": "101.25"}' Every write is checked against the whole history: a backdated sell that would leave the position below zero on any later date is refused (422), naming that date. An event dated in the future is refused too; record it once it has happened. Events are never edited. To correct one, reverse it (POST /position-events/<id /reverse) and record the right one with "replaces": "<id " (same date). The correction then takes the reversed event's place in that day. Without replaces, a new event goes after every event already recorded that day: re-recording an opening count after a buy on the same day would apply the count last and drop the buy. A position that holds nothing can be closed (PATCH /positions/<id with {"closed": true}, or Close on its row in the Positions tab); a closed position is read-only history. A position that holds nothing is not fetched, flagged stale or listed in the price status even before you close it. A new position in the same symbol starts after the closed one's last date (an earlier date is refused, 409), so the same shares are never counted twice.

sections.heading: Correct a closed position
sections.text: A position's last sale usually leaves it at zero, and once it is closed its events can no longer be reversed. To correct it: 1. Reopen it: PATCH /positions/<id with {"closed": false}, or reopen position(position id) from an agent (record sale answers with the position id, and the "position is closed" refusal names it). 2. Reverse the wrong event (POST /position-events/<id /reverse, or reverse position event(event id) from an agent); a sale's cash is undone with it. 3. Record the right event. 4. Close it again ({"closed": true}). The reopen is refused (409) while another position in the same symbol is open on the account, or when a later position in the symbol exists: its history follows this one's, so correct that one instead.

sections.heading: Sales and purchases move cash
sections.text: A sale puts its net proceeds (quantity x price - fees, rounded to the cent) on the account on the trade date, the day its shares leave the holdings, so net worth does not dip in between. To post the cash on a later settlement date instead, give settle on (settle date from an agent). From an agent, record sale records it; check first with dry run=true, which answers with the shares before and after, the cash and its date, and writes nothing: record sale(account="assets.plan", symbol="ACME", quantity="20", price="101.25", trade date="2026-10-01", fees="4.95", dry run=true) Then the same call without dry run. Over REST, record a sell event on the position: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/positions/<position id /events \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"kind": "sell", "occurred on": "2026-10-01", "quantity": "20", "price": "101.25", "fees": "4.95"}' - The cash is one ordinary transaction, posted, booked against the system account equity.securities. That account is not a category: the proceeds never count as income or spending, and net worth does not move: by default the cash posts on the trade date, the day the shares leave the holdings. (A later settle on, or a linked bank row dated after the trade, leaves net worth short by the sale's value until that date; see below.) The row waits for review like any other row Purser posts, and the register shows it as Securities trade . - proceeds to: "none" records a sale without cash, such as shares withheld for tax. - Trade cash is in US dollars only (equity.securities is a USD account, and Purser keeps one currency per transaction). On an account in another currency, a trade that would move cash is refused: record it with proceeds to: "none" or funded from: "none". - A buy takes its cost (quantity x price + fees, rounded to the cent) off the account only with funded from: "cash". By default a buy moves no cash: plan purchases are usually funded by payroll, from outside the account.

sections.heading: When the account already shows the cash
sections.text: Many brokers send the sale's cash through the feed ("SOLD ..."). Purser looks for a row of exactly that amount on the account, pending or posted, with one other leg, a category (so not a transfer or a split), dated from the trade to five days after settlement (settle on, or the next business day when you give none). When it finds one, the sale is refused with cash already recorded (a 409 over REST, a tool error led by that code from record sale), naming the row, so the cash is never counted twice; a record sale dry run reports the row as already recorded. If the row is still pending, record the sale after the bank posts it and link the posted row. If that row is the sale's cash, link it (transaction id="<the row " on record sale, or over REST): curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/positions/<position id /events \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"kind": "sell", "occurred on": "2026-10-01", "quantity": "20", "price": "101.25", "transaction id": "<the row the 409 named "}' which re-books that row to equity.securities as the sale's cash (the row is corrected through a reversal pair; its amount and date stay the bank's, and the sale settles on that date). The shares still leave on the trade date; until the bank's date the sale's cash counts as in transit (see below), so net worth does not dip. A link takes only the row that holds exactly this sale's cash: its net proceeds to the cent (so give the price, and the fees that produced the bank's figure), dated from the trade to five days after the next business day (settle on does not widen a link's window), and matched to no bill. Any other row is refused (422). When the row's bank line settles a bill, the refusal names the match: reject it if it is a proposal, unmatch it if it is confirmed, then link. If the row is a different payment that merely has the same amount, record the sale again with force cash: true (force cash=true on record sale): Purser posts the sale's cash as well, and the trade's audit record notes the override and the row it went past. record sale names that row too, as cash probe overridden, in its answer and in a dry run with force cash. A trade's cash moves only with its trade. Its row cannot be edited or recategorized, merged into a transfer or matched to a bill, and neither can the bank row a trade linked. Reversing the sale undoes the cash too, the way every posted row is corrected (a reversal and its replacement): Purser's own row is corrected to zero, so the register keeps it at 0.00 as the record of the undo, and a linked row gets its old category back.

sections.heading: When the broker's row arrives after the sale
sections.text: If you record the sale before the broker's "SOLD" row reaches Purser, Purser posts the cash itself. When the feed then delivers a row of exactly that amount on the account, dated from the trade to five days after settlement (the later of settle on and the next business day), the import links it as the sale's cash in place of Purser's own row, the same way transaction id links one: the cash is counted once, and the row keeps the bank's date and description. Purser's row stays in the history as void, pointing at the bank's row. The sync result counts these rows as linked trade cash. While the broker's row is still pending it is not imported at all (skipped trade cash pending); the posted row takes over when the bank books it. This works on every import, including an outage repair and a manual refetch. Reversing the sale later gives the bank's row back the category it was imported with, so the bank's money stays on the account as an ordinary deposit. A row outside that window, or of another amount, imports as an ordinary row. If that leaves the cash counted twice, reverse the sale's event and record it again with transaction id naming the feed's row. On an account that has "Feed balance is cash" on, the drift check shows such a gap.

sections.heading: Cash in transit
sections.text: The shares leave the holdings on the trade date, but the cash can land later: on settle on when you give a later date, or on the bank's date when the cash is the broker's row. Until the cash lands, Purser counts it as in transit: the position's holdings row carries it in its market value, and list holdings and GET /holdings show it as in transit (a sale's proceeds positive, a cash-funded buy's cost negative). Net worth therefore stays the same across a sale at the market price, on every day, including weekends between a Friday trade and a Monday bank row. After a sale of every share, the position still shows a zero-share line worth the cash until the cash date. unrealized gain covers the shares only.

sections.heading: Check a cash sweep's balance
sections.text: Some plan accounts reach SimpleFIN as a cash sweep: the feed's balance is the sweep's cash, not the account's value. For such an account, an admin can turn on Feed balance is cash (admin only; PATCH /accounts/<id with {"feed balance is cash": true}). Each sync then compares the feed's balance with the account's transactions, exactly as it does for a checking account, and reports drift in Settings - Connections , as balance.drift events and in whats new. That is how a missing sale shows up: while the proceeds that funded the disbursements are unrecorded, the account's transactions fall short of the sweep's balance by exactly that much. Recording the sales closes the gap. The setting needs manual holdings and turns off when the account goes back to the feed. It is off by default because many brokers report the account's total value as its balance.

sections.heading: Prices
sections.text: Each position is valued at the newest close for its symbol, from three sources: 1. a close you record: record price(symbol, date, close) or POST /prices; 2. the daily provider fetch, when a provider is configured; 3. a price implied by a feed snapshot of the same symbol in another account (its market value over its quantity). The newest date wins. The order above only breaks a tie between closes of the same date, so a close you recorded months ago never outlives newer ones. A feed-implied price is dated by the day the bank was fetched, not the trading session it reflects, so it ranks lower: it wins over a close you recorded or the provider's only when that close is more than seven days older. And while the bank keeps reporting the same value, the price keeps the date it first appeared, so a bank whose value is frozen turns stale like any other price. A position with no price at all adds nothing to the balance, and the surfaces say so (no price in list holdings, "no price" in the UI). It is never counted as zero. Neither does a position whose value at its close is too large to store, which almost always means a mistyped share count: the surfaces flag it as value out of range ("check the share count" in the UI), and recording a close does not change it; correct the count instead.

sections.heading: Configure a provider
sections.text: Settings - Prices sets the provider, its API key and the staleness threshold: - Provider : none (the default: record closes by hand) or tiingo (end-of-day closes; a free key is enough). The provider sees ticker symbols only, never quantities, accounts or values. - API key : write-only and encrypted in Purser's database. There is no environment variable for it, and it never appears in a response or a log. A key with a space, a line break or a non-ASCII character is refused when you save it. - Stale after : a position whose newest close is older than this many days (default 7) is flagged stale. The fetch runs daily at 06:40 UTC. It fetches every date your positions hold shares (from a week before each position's first day, so a weekend start gets the Friday close) that the provider has not answered yet, including positions you have closed, and later only what is new. When the history grows (you backdate an event, or another account held the symbol at another time), the next run fetches the missing dates, wherever they fall. Dates the provider has nothing for (before a symbol listed, a weekend) are asked for once. Fetch now runs the same job on demand. One failing ticker, or one failing date range, never blocks the others: it records a price.fetch failed event and the rest carry on. Tiingo spells share classes with a dash, so a position recorded as BRK.B is fetched as BRK-B.

sections.heading: Price a plan-only fund
sections.text: Some plans' feeds send a fund they hold but cannot value: an employer plan's collective trust, say, which no market-data provider prices. The feed reports the shares with a market value of 0, or with none at all, so the position would add nothing to the balance. You do not need to track that account by hand for it: record the fund's unit price, and Purser values the feed's row from it on read. record price(symbol="ACMEX", date="2026-10-16", close="23.4") or over REST: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/prices \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"symbol": "ACMEX", "date": "2026-10-16", "close": "23.4"}' - Record the price under the fund's ticker. The feed's symbol is matched the way Purser stores a ticker (spaces trimmed, upper case), so acmex in the feed takes the price recorded for ACMEX. - A feed that sends a description instead of a ticker (Stable Value Trust, say) cannot be priced: no recorded price matches it. Such a position is flagged unpriceable (in list holdings, GET /holdings and whats new) and adds nothing; there is nothing to record for it. - Any feed row of that symbol that holds shares with no value (0 or none) is worth shares × the newest price dated on or before the row's date. A price you record wins over a provider's of the same date. The feed's stored row never changes, and a value the feed does send is never overridden. - Recording a price for an earlier date re-values the account's history from that date; net worth heals by itself. - Weekly is enough: the newest price carries forward, and once it is older than the staleness threshold (Settings, Prices) the fund is reported stale like a hand-tracked one: stale in list holdings, a price.stale event, Settings - Prices and whats new's stale prices. - Until a price exists, the position shows no price (no price in list holdings, market value null), never a silent 0, and whats new reports it once (unpriced holdings). - No provider is asked for such a symbol: the price comes from the plan's site.

sections.heading: Tax lots and equity awards
sections.text: A hand-tracked position can also track its tax lots (acquisition date, remaining shares, basis), and the account its equity awards and vest schedule. A position's basis then comes from its lots, never an average, and a sale names the lots it draws on. Lot lists and award schedules load in bulk with a previewed, idempotent capture. See Track tax lots and equity awards.

sections.heading: Where the value shows up
sections.text: Hand-tracked positions are written into the same holdings snapshots table the feed fills, so everything that reads holdings picks them up unchanged: - the account's balance is its cash plus its holdings' market value (balance method: "postings+holdings"), on every account surface; - net worth, balance history and the Grafana dashboards include it; - list holdings lists each brokerage account with its source, its value, and how many positions are on a stale close (stale price) or have no price (no price); named one account, it pages through its positions with their cost basis, in symbol order (cursor, next cursor). A page never repeats a position, but each page reads the account's newest set when it is called: a position added meanwhile with a symbol before the cursor is not listed, and the daily price job can move later pages to a newer set; - whats new reports symbols whose price turned stale (stale prices) and feed positions no price values yet (unpriced holdings). See Balances for how the postings and holdings figures combine, and Events and webhooks for position.updated, price.stale, price.fetch failed and holding.unpriced. Agents record share counts with record position and sales with record sale, and undo a wrong one with reverse position event (reopening a closed position first with reopen position); buys and closing a position are REST (or the admin UI's Positions tab, for share counts and closing).

pages.title: Single sign-on with OIDC
pages.description: Wire Purser to a generic OpenID provider (Authentik as the example) with three runtime-editable settings that can never lock you out.

sections.text: Purser can authenticate admins against any generic OpenID Connect provider. Authentik is the worked example below, but the three settings are standard OIDC and apply to any compliant provider.

sections.heading: Register Purser with your provider
sections.text: Create an OAuth2/OpenID application in your provider (a confidential client, authorization code flow) and set its redirect URI to, exactly, your PURSER PUBLIC URL followed by /auth/oidc/callback. The redirect base is your instance's PURSER PUBLIC URL — which is environment-only, since it also drives cookie security.
