If PURSER PUBLIC URL is https://purser.example.com, register https://purser.example.com/auth/oidc/callback. Note the client id and client secret your provider issues.

sections.heading: The three settings
sections.text: Set the issuer, client id, and client secret. SSO enables only when all three are present : Setting Value --- --- PURSER OIDC ISSUER Your provider's issuer URL (e.g. an Authentik application's OpenID configuration base). PURSER OIDC CLIENT ID The client id from the provider. PURSER OIDC CLIENT SECRET The client secret (write-only: encrypted at rest, never echoed back, masked to set/unset in audit rows). These are runtime-editable in Settings - Security (or the admin-scoped /config API); the environment values are just the bootstrap default, and a database override wins. Every change is audited.

sections.heading: Who gets in
sections.text: An SSO identity is the provider's issuer together with the subject (sub) it issues: the same subject at another provider is another person. An identity already linked to a Purser user signs straight in. Otherwise Purser looks for an account with the id token's email, ignoring letter case, and only when the provider asserts email verified in the id token. An unverified email is refused: a provider that issues tokens with subject-chosen emails must not be able to take over a local account. The account with that email What happens --- --- Is not linked to SSO It links to this identity on first sign-in (audited user.link oidc). Is linked through another provider It relinks to this identity (audited user.link oidc, with the previous issuer). This is how you move to a new provider. Is linked to another subject of this provider Refused with 403 "this account is linked to a different SSO identity; ask an administrator to unlink it", and audited user.link oidc refused. Nothing changes. Does not exist Refused with "account not provisioned" by default. Pre-create the user in the admin UI (matching the verified email), or set PURSER OIDC AUTO PROVISION (also runtime-editable) to auto-create member accounts, again only for verified emails. email verified must be the JSON boolean true; a string "true" counts as unverified. An account stays linked to its identity: a later change of email at the provider does not move it. So only connect a provider that verifies the emails it marks as verified. Emails match regardless of letter case everywhere: SSO linking, auto-provisioning, password sign-in and the rule that every account has its own email. Purser keeps each email as it was entered.

sections.heading: Unlink an SSO identity
sections.text: When someone's identity at your provider changes (a recreated account, a new subject), Purser refuses it until an admin unlinks the old one. On the Users page, choose Unlink SSO on that user's row; over the API it is DELETE /users/{user id}/oidc with an admin token. The account, its password if it has one, and its history stay; the next SSO sign-in that asserts the account's verified email links it again. The unlink is audited user.unlink oidc with the admin as actor. Unlinking a user who has no SSO link answers 409. Links made before Purser recorded the provider were attributed to the provider configured at upgrade time. If none was configured then, such a link counts as belonging to whichever provider is configured now: its own subject signs in and records the provider, and any other subject is refused until you unlink it.

sections.heading: Move to another provider
sections.text: 1. Make sure the new provider asserts verified emails that match your Purser accounts (letter case does not matter). 2. Change the issuer, client id and client secret in Settings - Security . 3. Each person signs in through the new provider once. Their account relinks to the new identity, audited with the previous issuer. Accounts nobody signs in with stay linked to the old provider until they do, or until an admin unlinks them. Moving back to a provider you used before works the same way.

sections.heading: What Purser checks
sections.text: Each sign-in is an authorization code flow with three per-attempt secrets, kept in a short-lived cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, ten minutes). When PURSER PUBLIC URL is https://, it is Host-purser oidc state with Secure and Path=/: browsers accept that prefix only from this exact host, so a sibling subdomain cannot plant a sign-in attempt of its own. On plain HTTP, where the prefix is unavailable, it is purser oidc state, scoped to /auth/oidc. - state ties the provider's redirect back to the browser that started the sign-in, so a link to someone else's callback is refused. - nonce must come back unchanged inside the id token. - PKCE (S256): the code exchange carries the verifier, so a code seen in transit is useless on its own. The provider's discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration under the issuer) must name the issuer you configured; a trailing slash is the only difference allowed. When the issuer is https://, its authorization, token and JWKS endpoints must be https:// too. Discovery and the signing keys are fetched for every sign-in, so a key rotation at the provider takes effect at once. Every request to the provider has a 10-second timeout and does not follow redirects. The id token from the token endpoint must then pass: Check Rule --- --- Signature RS256 or ES256, by a key from the provider's JWKS selected by kid (a token without a kid is accepted only when the JWKS has one key). none, the HMAC algorithms and any other algorithm are refused, as is a key published for encryption or of the wrong type. iss Equal to the discovery document's issuer. aud / azp aud contains the client id. A token for several audiences needs azp equal to the client id; any azp must be the client id. exp Required; the token is refused once it has expired, with no grace period. iat, nbf iat is required. Up to 60 seconds of clock difference with the provider is tolerated for a token stamped slightly in the future. sub, nonce sub is a non-empty string; nonce matches this sign-in. email Required, a string. Unknown header parameters are ignored unless the token lists them in crit.

sections.heading: When sign-in fails
sections.text: The callback answers with a fixed message and logs the failing check, never a code or token: Status Meaning --- --- 400 The state did not match (an expired, missing or foreign sign-in attempt), the callback had no code, or the provider reported an error such as a cancelled sign-in. Start again from the login page. 401 The id token failed one of the checks above. The log line oidc.id token rejected names which. 403 The token was valid but Purser refused the account (see "Who gets in"). 502 The provider could not be reached, or answered something unusable: discovery, the JWKS or the token exchange failed (log line oidc.provider error, with the step). A wrong client secret shows up here.

sections.heading: It can never lock you out
sections.text: OIDC is safe to edit live. The OIDC client is rebuilt per request and password login is always available as an independent fallback , so a wrong issuer or a bad secret cannot lock the admin out — you log in with a password and fix the value. An explicit null override on the issuer or client id is the kill switch: it disables SSO even when the environment configures it.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.text: With all three set, the login page offers an SSO button that redirects to your provider and back through the callback URI above. If the round trip fails, log in with a password, open Settings - Security , and re-check the issuer URL and the redirect URI registered at the provider — those two are the usual culprits. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 9 (security model); every setting is listed in Configuration.

pages.title: Reconcile an account
pages.description: Match an account to its statement balance, see what Purser posts and records, and how a reconciliation stays honest when history changes afterwards.

sections.text: Reconciling tells Purser "the statement says this account held X at the end of this date". Purser compares X with its own balance for that date, posts one adjustment for any difference, and records the claim. From then on, every read of the account re-checks the claim, so a reconciled balance never goes stale silently.

sections.heading: Which accounts
sections.text: Checking, savings, cash and credit-card accounts. These are the accounts whose balance is the sum of their transactions. Manual brokerage accounts can reconcile cash only with explicit component: "cash". Enter the broker's cash balance, excluding securities and unvested awards; never enter total account value. Feed brokerage accounts must first be switched to manual holdings by an administrator. Other eligible accounts use component: "balance" (the default). For example, cash of -100.00 in the ledger and a reported cash balance of 25.00 produce a 125.00 adjustment. Holdings worth 1000.00 remain unchanged, so total owned value becomes 1025.00. Unvested awards remain outside net worth. A hand-valued asset (type property: a house, a car) reconciles to its value on the date: the difference posts against the system account equity.revaluation as a change in value, not to the adjustments category (see Track a house or other asset). A loan balance is a valuation. Record a valuation for a loan instead, with POST /accounts/{id}/valuations or the MCP tool record valuation (see Recording a valuation). Reconciling a credit card checks what the card owed on the statement date; it does not change what you plan to pay. To make the upcoming card payment the statement balance, record it on the payment instead (see Card statement balances).

sections.heading: Enter the balance as the statement shows it
sections.text: Pass statement balance exactly as it is printed, and Purser converts it: Account The statement shows You enter Purser's ledger balance --- --- --- --- Checking, savings, cash 1250.00 in the account "1250.00" 1250.0000 Credit card 425.00 owed "425.00" -425.0000 Credit card a 10.00 credit balance "-10.00" 10.0000 Purser keeps a card's balance negative when you owe money, so a statement's positive amount owed is negated on the way in. Every amount in the answer is in the ledger's sign, except statement balance, which echoes what you entered.

sections.heading: Pick the basis
sections.text: Banks report one of two balances, so say which one the statement shows: - posted (the default) counts cleared transactions only. This is the usual statement balance. - pending inclusive also counts pending transactions. It matches the "current balance" many banking sites show. A pending hold dated before the statement date counts in pending inclusive and not in posted.

sections.heading: Preview, then reconcile
sections.text: For a read-only check first, use MCP account balance or GET /accounts/{id}/balance. Their bank snapshot exposes the bank-reported and available balances with ordinary read access. It is the latest feed snapshot, not a statement balance at your requested as of date, and its comparison uses all live posting dates. Do not reconcile an old statement from that live difference. Available balance is a separate bank quantity, not the reconciliation target. See Bank balance reads. POST /accounts/{id}/reconcile needs write scope. Start with a dry run. It runs the same computation, conflicts included, and writes nothing: { "as of": "2026-09-30", "statement balance": "1250.00", "basis": "posted", "dry run": true } { "reconciliation id": null, "account id": "3f6c1e52-1b1e-4c55-9a7e-0b8f5d2a7c41", "as of": "2026-09-30", "basis": "posted", "component": "balance", "statement balance": "1250.0000", "target balance": "1250.0000", "ledger balance": "1225.0000", "adjustment": "25.0000", "adjustment tx id": null, "category": "expenses.reconciliation adjustments", "reconciled through": "2026-09-30", "created": false, "dry run": true } ledger balance is Purser's balance on that date before any adjustment, and adjustment is what it will post. If the adjustment is not what you expect, look for a missing or duplicated transaction before you commit. Then send the same body without dry run. The answer is the same, with created: true and the new ids. as of is the statement date, today (in the household time zone, UTC by default) or earlier. A future date is rejected.

sections.heading: What Purser records
sections.text: - One adjustment, when needed. A difference becomes one ordinary posted transaction dated on the statement date, in the category expenses.reconciliation adjustments, with the payee "Balance reconciliation". It lands in the unreviewed set, so you see every adjustment, including one an agent made. If you later find what it was, recategorize it like any other transaction. The account balance does not change. - A clean reconcile too. When the ledger already matches, nothing is posted, and the reconciliation is still recorded with an adjustment of 0. - The marker. The account's reconciled through moves to the statement date. - An audit row and an event. Every reconciliation writes an audit row and emits account.reconciled.

sections.heading: When history changes later
sections.text: A transaction dated on or before a reconciled date can still arrive or change after you reconcile: a late import, an edit or correction, or a pending hold that disappears. Purser does not rewrite the reconciliation when that happens. It re-checks the claim every time you read it: - GET /accounts/{id} (and the accounts list) carries reconciliation, the latest reconciliation with ledger balance (the balance on that date now), difference (ledger balance minus target) and in balance. The component identifies cash-only brokerage claims. A changing share price cannot move a cash reconciliation; a backdated cash transaction can. - GET /accounts/{id}/reconciliations lists every reconciliation, newest first, each re-checked the same way. - The agent tool list accounts carries the same check for each reconciled account. For example, you reconcile September 30 to 1250.00, and then a 10.00 deposit dated September 29 imports late. The reconciliation now reads "in balance": false, "difference": "10.0000". To resolve it, find the change. If it was entered by mistake, correct it, and the reconciliation reads in balance again. If it is real, the adjustment posted at the time was probably standing in for it. Reconcile the next statement: its adjustment nets the difference out, and the older reconciliation stays visible as out of balance.

sections.heading: Retries and conflicts
sections.text: Retrying is safe. The same date, balance and basis returns the recorded result with created: false while the ledger still matches. Once the ledger has moved, the retry fails with 409 instead of looking like a success. The response body detail says why: detail.code Meaning --- --- reconciliation moved This reconciliation is recorded, but the balance on that date has changed since. detail.difference is the ledger balance minus the target. reconciliation conflict A different balance or basis is already recorded for that date. Each account has at most one reconciliation per date. reconciliation out of order The date is before the account's latest reconciliation. Reconcile that date or a later one.

sections.heading: For agents
sections.text: The MCP tool reconcile account takes the same inputs and needs write scope. account is a UUID or a path: { "account": "liabilities.card", "as of": "2026-09-30", "statement balance": "425.00", "dry run": true } Do a dry run first, read adjustment back to the user, and commit only when they agree. Never flip a card statement's sign yourself. Purser does that. A loan statement is not reconciled. Record its figure with the MCP tool record valuation (write scope), entered as printed, with convention set to statement: { "account": "liabilities.mortgage", "as of": "2026-09-30", "value": "250000.00", "convention": "statement" } Purser stores -250000.0000, the ledger sign of an amount owed, and reports it as the loan's balance from then on. Without convention, value is read in the ledger's sign, so a positive figure on a loan is refused rather than recorded as an asset. Here too, never flip the sign yourself. The design and its trade-offs are in DESIGN.md section 3.7 and decision 61.

pages.title: Put Purser behind a reverse proxy
pages.description: Serve Purser over HTTPS with Caddy, nginx or Traefik, keep port 8000 private, trust only the proxy's forwarded headers, and keep MCP streaming and imports working.

sections.text: Purser serves plain HTTP on port 8000. For anything beyond the machine it runs on, put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of it. This page gives working examples for Caddy, nginx and Traefik with the Docker Compose setup, then explains each setting they depend on. Serve Purser at the root of its own host name, such as https://purser.example.com. A path prefix (https://example.com/purser) is not supported: the web UI, the API and /mcp all use root-absolute paths.

sections.heading: What every setup needs
sections.text: 1. PURSER PUBLIC URL is the HTTPS address , exactly as people and agents type it: https://purser.example.com, with no path. 2. Port 8000 stays private. Keep PURSER BIND ADDRESS at its default, 127.0.0.1, so only the proxy reaches Purser. 3. The proxy forwards the original Host , sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, and passes the browser's Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site headers through unchanged. 4. Purser trusts the forwarded headers from the proxy's address only , through FORWARDED ALLOW IPS. 5. The proxy allows request bodies up to 32 MiB , and does not buffer the MCP endpoint's streamed responses. Caddy and Traefik meet points 3 and 5 with their defaults; nginx needs the settings shown below.

sections.heading: Give Purser a fixed network address
sections.text: Inside the container, Purser never sees a request as coming from 127.0.0.1. A proxy on the Docker host reaches it through the published port, so requests arrive from the gateway address of the Compose network; a proxy running in Compose connects from its own container address. Docker assigns both when it creates the network, so pin the network's address range in docker-compose.override.yml (next to docker-compose.yml; see Keep your changes in an override file). Pick a private range that nothing else on your network uses: docker-compose.override.yml, for a proxy installed on the Docker host services: purser: environment: FORWARDED ALLOW IPS: 172.30.80.1 networks: default: ipam: config: - subnet: 172.30.80.0/24 gateway: 172.30.80.1 Docker applies a new address range only to a new network, so recreate it once: docker compose down (without -v, which would delete your data), then docker compose up -d.

sections.heading: Caddy
sections.text: Caddy installed on the Docker host obtains and renews the certificate itself. The whole Caddyfile: purser.example.com { reverse proxy 127.0.0.1:8000 } In .env: PURSER PUBLIC URL=https://purser.example.com PURSER BIND ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 Caddy forwards the original Host, sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, sends server-sent event responses on without buffering, and sets no request body limit. Use the override file from Give Purser a fixed network address.

sections.heading: nginx
sections.text: nginx installed on the Docker host, with a certificate you manage (for example with certbot). Use the same .env values and override file as for Caddy: server { listen 80; server name purser.example.com; return 301 https://$host$request uri; } server { listen 443 ssl; http2 on; server name purser.example.com; ssl certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/purser.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl certificate key /etc/letsencrypt/live/purser.example.com/privkey.pem; Purser accepts bodies up to 32 MiB (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES). nginx's own default is 1 MiB, too small for a long QIF or CSV import. client max body size 32m; location / { proxy pass http://127.0.0.1:8000; proxy set header Host $host; proxy set header X-Forwarded-For $proxy add x forwarded for; proxy set header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; } MCP answers each request with a server-sent event stream: pass it on as it arrives, and allow slow tool calls to finish. location /mcp { proxy pass http://127.0.0.1:8000; proxy set header Host $host; proxy set header X-Forwarded-For $proxy add x forwarded for; proxy set header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy http version 1.1; proxy set header Connection ""; proxy buffering off; proxy cache off; proxy read timeout 300s; } } http2 on; needs nginx 1.25.1 or later; on an older nginx, write listen 443 ssl http2; instead. Check the file with nginx -t before reloading.

sections.heading: Traefik with Compose labels
sections.text: Traefik can run as another service in the same Compose project and find Purser through container labels. This override file adds Traefik with a Let's Encrypt certificate, routes purser.example.com to Purser, and gives Traefik a fixed address for FORWARDED ALLOW IPS: docker-compose.override.yml, with Traefik in the same project services: traefik: image: traefik:v3.6 restart: unless-stopped command: - --providers.docker=true - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false - --entrypoints.web.address=:80 - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.to=websecure - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.scheme=https - --entrypoints.websecure.address=:443 - --certificatesresolvers.letsencrypt.acme.tlschallenge=true - --certificatesresolvers.letsencrypt.acme.email=admin@example.com - --certificatesresolvers.letsencrypt.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json ports: - "80:80" - "443:443" volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro - traefik-letsencrypt:/letsencrypt networks: default: ipv4 address: 172.30.80.10 purser: environment: FORWARDED ALLOW IPS: 172.30.80.10 labels: - traefik.enable=true - traefik.http.routers.purser.rule=Host(purser.example.com) - traefik.http.routers.purser.entrypoints=websecure - traefik.http.routers.purser.tls.certresolver=letsencrypt - traefik.http.services.purser.loadbalancer.server.port=8000 networks: default: ipam: config: - subnet: 172.30.80.0/24 volumes: traefik-letsencrypt: In .env, set PURSER PUBLIC URL=https://purser.example.com and keep PURSER BIND ADDRESS=127.0.0.1: Traefik reaches Purser over the Compose network, so the published port only serves the host itself. Traefik forwards the original Host, sets the forwarded headers, streams responses and sets no body limit by default. Access to the Docker socket gives Traefik control of Docker, even read-only; a socket proxy narrows that if it concerns you. If you also run the worker separately, give it no labels.

sections.heading: PURSER_PUBLIC_URL
sections.text: Purser reads PURSER PUBLIC URL at startup; run docker compose up -d after changing it. It decides: - Secure cookies. An https:// address marks the session cookie Secure, so the browser never sends it over plain HTTP. - The single sign-on address. The redirect address Purser sends to your identity provider is PURSER PUBLIC URL followed by /auth/oidc/callback, for example https://purser.example.com/auth/oidc/callback. Register exactly that with the provider; see Single sign-on with OIDC. - The MCP endpoint's allowed host. /mcp accepts requests only for the public host and local addresses such as localhost, and answers any other Host with 421 Misdirected Request. A mismatch between the address an agent uses and PURSER PUBLIC URL shows up as 421 errors in the agent. - Links. Links that tools return for you to open in the web UI start with this address.

sections.heading: Forwarded headers and FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS
sections.text: The image runs Purser under uvicorn, which honours X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto only from the addresses listed in its own FORWARDED ALLOW IPS variable (default 127.0.0.1,::1). It accepts single addresses and networks such as 172.30.80.0/24. Purser uses the resulting client address for sign-in throttling and records it on failed sign-ins in the audit log. List the proxy's address and nothing else. Any address on the list can claim to be any client, so never use , and do not list a network that untrusted machines share. If the proxy's address is missing from the list, every request appears to come from the proxy: the per-address sign-in limit then counts all failed sign-ins together, and a password-guessing attack pauses password sign-in for everyone until the lockout ends. To check it, make one failed sign-in from another machine and look at the auth.login failed entry in the audit log: it should show that machine's address, not the proxy's.

sections.heading: Host, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site
sections.text: The web UI signs you in with a session cookie, and Purser refuses (403) a write made with that cookie when the browser reports another site sent it: Sec-Fetch-Site other than same-origin or none, or, without that header, an Origin that is not Purser's own address. See Requests from other sites. A proxy that rewrites or replaces Origin therefore breaks saving in the web UI. Forward the original Host too: it is what the MCP allowlist checks.

sections.heading: Request body size
sections.text: Purser refuses request bodies larger than 32 MiB with 413 (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES). A proxy's own limit applies first, so set it at least as high. Caddy and Traefik set none by default; nginx defaults to 1 MiB, which is why the example sets client max body size 32m. A QIF or CSV import larger than the proxy's limit fails with a 413 from the proxy before Purser sees it.

sections.heading: MCP streaming
sections.text: /mcp uses MCP's streamable HTTP transport without sessions: each request is a POST, and Purser answers it with a server-sent event stream (text/event-stream) that closes when the answer is complete. A proxy that buffers responses holds the stream back until it ends, so turn buffering off for /mcp (proxy buffering off in nginx). Long tool calls keep the response open; allow them more than nginx's default 60 second read timeout. An agent may call /mcp without the trailing slash; Purser redirects it to /mcp/, so route the whole /mcp prefix to Purser.

sections.heading: Check the result
sections.text: From another machine: curl https://purser.example.com/healthz Expected: {"status":"ok","database":"ok"}. Then sign in to the web UI over HTTPS, change a setting to confirm that writes are accepted, and connect an agent to https://purser.example.com/mcp (see Connect an agent).

sections.heading: Related
sections.text: - Run with Docker Compose: the compose files, .env and the override file. - Configuration: PURSER PUBLIC URL, PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES and sign-in throttling. - Deploy on Kubernetes with Helm: the same settings with an ingress. - Security model: sessions, cross-site writes and throttling.

pages.title: Review new transactions
pages.description: Rows that arrive without human eyes form an unreviewed set over your registers — how to work through it yourself, with an agent, or automatically.

sections.text: Some rows land in your ledger without anyone looking at them: transactions the SimpleFIN feed imports, and transfers Purser merges on its own. Those form the unreviewed set . It is a filter over your existing registers, not a second inbox. Purser deliberately replaced its review queue with per-account registers, and this does not bring the queue back — a row is simply flagged until something looks at it.

sections.heading: What is in the set
sections.text: Only rows that arrived unattended: - transactions imported from the feed ; - transfers Purser merged automatically ; - replacements produced by a rule ; - adjustments Purser posts when you reconcile an account, whoever asked for the reconcile. Your own imports are not included. A QIF or CSV file you chose to import is not something you need reminding to review, so a 6,000-row Quicken import adds nothing to the set. Neither do rows your agent writes: each is attributed to its token in the audit log and marked agent-made in the register. Upcoming rows a schedule expects are not in it either. An expected bill or paycheck is a forecast, not something that happened; when the bank row it predicted arrives, that row is the one to review. Everything that existed before this feature shipped counts as reviewed, so it starts quiet and only ever concerns rows that arrive from now on.

sections.heading: Rows leave the set on their own
sections.text: You usually do not have to mark anything. A row clears when anything you or your agent does touches it : editing it, posting it, confirming a transfer, confirming a match or matching it to an expected row by hand. The action is the review. Automation is different. A rule that recategorizes a row, the nightly categorization pass, or a match Purser confirms on its own leaves it needing review — automation touching a row is not the same as someone checking it. That is the whole point of the flag. A review follows the bank line . When a pending row you reviewed (or confirmed a match on) posts, the posted row arrives already reviewed — who reviewed it, when, the note and any flag come along — as long as it carries the same category you saw on the pending. If the posted row lands in a different category, it needs review again, because that category is something nobody has looked at. A row the bank posts after you never reviewed its pending stays in the set. A merged transfer is a new judgement of its own, so merging rows into a transfer never carries their review.

sections.heading: Working through it
sections.text: In the UI, unreviewed rows carry a needs review badge in their register, and the dashboard shows how many are outstanding. Both come from the same server-side check, so they always agree. Over the REST API, each row from GET /transactions (and a single transaction's detail) carries it as needs review; read that rather than treating a missing reviewed at as unreviewed, because rows outside the set never get a mark. From an agent, review batch returns the next rows with everything needed to judge them inline — current category and who chose it, any transfer on the row, the raw-versus-friendly payee, what automation did — plus a short checklist. There are no per-row round-trips by design; a reviewer that has to fetch context row by row will skip it. Then mark reviewed closes the loop, in bulk and idempotently.

sections.heading: Check what context was available
sections.text: Every batch reports a context map saying which surfaces it could actually offer. If something a decision needed was unavailable, that batch's rows were reviewed with less information than they look like they had — so the guidance says to escalate rather than clear in that case.

sections.heading: Escalating
sections.text: A reviewer that is unsure can mark a row reviewed and flag it for you. The row leaves the unreviewed set — no second queue appears — but shows a flagged badge and carries a note explaining why. The clearest case is an ambiguous transfer: categorizing a row as [account path] names an account, not a specific row, so when two rows in that account could be its pair, the right move is to hand it back rather than guess.

sections.heading: Rows a securities trade holds
sections.text: A sale's cash on a hand-tracked brokerage account, and the bank's row a sale linked as its cash, are flagged securities trade and carry locked, which names the trade (event id) and its position (position id). Such a row moves only with its trade, so recategorizing it or confirming it as a transfer is refused. Mark it reviewed if the trade is right; if it is wrong, reverse the trade's event (reopening a closed position first) and record it again. The batch's guidance says the same, so a later page fetched with include guidance=false carries only the marker. See Manual holdings.

sections.heading: Letting Purser review it for you
sections.text: If you have configured an AI provider, you can have the review pass run server-side instead of waiting for a connected agent. It is off by default and needs its own switch — configuring a provider grants nothing on its own. When enabled, it runs after each sync, clears what the context supports, and escalates the rest, so your attention lands on the residue rather than the whole set. It is capped per run, and a provider failure simply leaves rows unreviewed rather than breaking the sync. Rows it clears are recorded as ai review, permanently distinguishable in the audit trail from a row you looked at yourself.

sections.heading: Nothing grows forever
sections.text: If reviewing lapses, rows older than PURSER REVIEW MAX AGE DAYS (90 by default) are auto-marked as aged by a nightly sweep. That is deliberately a different mark from a real review, so an audit reader can always tell which rows were actually examined — and the count is reported in your digest rather than clearing silently, because the sweep firing at all means review has lapsed.

sections.heading: Fixes that repeat should become rules
sections.text: The checklist ends with this and it is worth repeating: if you find yourself making the same correction over and over, that is a rule waiting to be written. These flags are the record of what your rules did not catch. See Write deterministic rules.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: - Write deterministic rules - Manage transfers - DESIGN.md section 4 (review marks) and decision 47

pages.title: Write deterministic rules
pages.description: Categorize, rename payees, and declare transfer pairs with rules that run automatically on new transactions — and never execute until you activate them.

sections.text: Rules are deterministic instructions Purser runs where automation already touches your rows: at import, and in the nightly sweep. They decide, so they are deliberately boring — no regex, no scoring, no fuzzy matching. A rule either matches or it does not, and you can read why off a single line. There are three kinds: - categorize — set a category, or name another real account to convert the row into a transfer, when a rule matches. - rename — map a raw bank descriptor to a friendly payee. - transfer link — declare that two accounts transfer to each other.

sections.heading: A rule never runs until you activate it
sections.text: A rule is created as a draft unless the call that creates it sets activate. Drafts are visible, editable and previewable, but they do not execute — the loader that feeds the import and sweep paths only ever selects active rules. An agent creates rules as drafts too, unless you asked it for the rule: then it may create it already active (propose rule with activate=true). A rule that is the agent's own idea stays a draft for you to decide. A pair (transfer link) rule is always created as a draft, because its activation confirms how many past pairs it will link (see below). Every rule write — creating, activating, editing or reaching back into history — needs the write scope and is recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Preview before you activate
sections.text: The predicate is the part worth checking, so preview it against your real history first: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/preview \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"match field": "payee", "match mode": "contains", "match text": "amazon"}' You get back how many live rows match, how many were scanned, and a sample. A count far larger than you expected is the signal that the predicate is too broad — narrow it with an account, an amount range, or a direction. A transfer link rule previews the same way, with its account pair instead of a predicate (see Declaring a transfer pair).

sections.heading: Matching is token-aware, not substring
sections.text: Text matching normalizes both sides and respects token boundaries, so a rule for an account named Chase does not fire on PURCHASE RETURN. Three modes: mode matches --- --- equals the whole normalized text prefix starts with the pattern, ending on a token boundary contains the pattern as a whole run of tokens prefix with star matches star market but not starbucks coffee. This makes a prefix rule useful for bank descriptors whose stable payee text is followed by a changing bill number or reference.

sections.heading: Everything you set is ANDed
sections.text: A predicate is the AND of whatever fields you set; unset fields are unconstrained. You can scope by account, by amount (amount exact, or an amount min/amount max range), by direction (debit or credit), and by effective from, which excludes rows dated strictly before it. direction reads the amount after any per-account sign inversion, so you write the rule in your sign world, not the bank's.

sections.heading: Which rule wins
sections.text: Rules of one kind are evaluated in priority order — lower numbers first — and the first match wins . GET /rules returns them in exactly that order, so resolution is visible before it fires rather than being something you deduce afterwards. Priority is a number you set, not something Purser infers from how specific a rule looks. That is on purpose: a rule's effect should be explainable by pointing at one row.

sections.heading: Map a payee durably
sections.text: For a durable payee mapping, use a categorize rule with match field: payee and choose the narrowest safe text mode. Its action target may be a virtual category such as expenses.utilities, or a real account such as liabilities.auto loan; a real target uses the same bracket-transfer conversion as an inline edit. Rules are the only automatic mapping from payee text that you configure, and they come first. Payee memory and the AI classifier (next section) only fill in rows no rule matched, and neither is a mapping you can edit. Nothing in the suggestions inbox applies a mapping itself either: the most a suggestion can do is propose one as a rule, which you accept through the same activation as a rule you write. That includes transfers: confirming a transfer by hand teaches Purser no hidden payee-to-account mapping — it proposes a transfer link rule (see A pair scoped to a payee).

sections.heading: Rules beat learned memory
sections.text: For categorization the order is: rule, then payee memory, then the AI classifier, then uncategorized A rule sits above the payee-to-category memory learned from your accepted history, so a rule can correct a memory that has gone wrong. If you find yourself fixing the same categorization repeatedly, that is the signal to graduate it into a rule.

sections.heading: Renaming consolidates history, not just new rows
sections.text: A rename rule rewrites the payee , never the bank's description — three different identity checks read that description, so rewriting it would corrupt them. Applying a rename to history does not rewrite your transactions. It aliases the payee itself, pointing the raw payees at the friendly one. Nothing about any posted row changes, and because payee memory counts rows across the whole alias group, consolidating several descriptors onto one payee makes that payee's memory stronger for everything that already happened. Clearing the alias undoes it.

sections.heading: Declaring a transfer pair
sections.text: Purser already links transfers automatically when the text carries a signal — a keyword like transfer or payment, or the counterparty account's name. Some real transfers carry neither. Recurring brokerage moves often arrive as opaque descriptors on both sides. A transfer link rule declares the account pair, and for that pair the name-signal requirement no longer applies. Everything else still does : the amounts must be exactly opposite, the two dates must fall inside the pair's window, both rows must be posted, and a pair you explicitly unlinked, or rejected as not a transfer, stays unlinked.

sections.heading: The pair's date window
sections.text: By default the two sides of a declared pair must post within 3 days of each other — the same window every other pair uses. Some transfers take longer: a card autopay that leaves checking on the 1st and lands on the card on the 5th is 4 days apart, and would stay unlinked. Set window days on the rule to give that pair, and only that pair , its own window: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"type": "transfer link", "pair account a": "CHECKING ID", "pair account b": "CARD ID", "amount exact": "184.50", "window days": 5}' - window days is a whole number of days from 0 (same day only) to 14. Leave it out for the standard 3 days. A value outside that range, a fraction, or a window days on any other kind of rule is refused with a 422. - It combines with amount exact and effective from, which narrow the pair as before. - A window below 3 narrows the pair: the rule vouches only for legs that post that close together. A name-signal pair still links within the standard 3 days, as it would without the rule. - A wider window never takes a row from a closer pair already in your ledger. Each pass first links everything inside the standard 3 days exactly as it would without the rule, and only then pairs the declared accounts farther apart, among the rows still without a partner. Every pair you did not declare keeps the 3-day window. Keep the window as narrow as the bank's real delay. Exact opposite amounts are the only other evidence a declared pair needs, and a wide window gives a stray equal amount more room to pair with the wrong row. A pair that repeats weekly should not go past 3.

sections.heading: A pair scoped to a payee
sections.text: A pair rule can be narrower than the whole pair. When you confirm a transfer by hand, Purser proposes a transfer link rule for those two accounts that only applies when one side of a pair carries the confirmed payee — see From a confirm to a rule. Accepting the suggestion creates that rule as a draft. Its predicate then reads a leg's payee is "..." or an alias, and GET /rules and MCP list rules show the payee as payee scope. Pairs between the same accounts with any other payee still need a name signal or a confirm. The scope follows the payee's aliases . When a rename's apply-history points the scope's payee at a friendlier one, or points other descriptors at it, rows under any payee in that group are covered and the rule shows the payee under its current name. A rename only merges payees through apply-history, and apply-history only aliases the payees of live rows. A payee whose rows have all been merged into transfers is not aliased, and neither is one whose rename only ever ran on new rows. Rows under the new name then fall outside the scope; confirm one of those pairs and Purser proposes a rule for the new name. The payee scope is part of what an active rule links, like its window: an active rule refuses an edit that would drop or change it. Rules you write yourself declare the whole pair; a payee scope comes from an accepted suggestion. Preview a pair before you create the rule: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/preview \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"pair account a": "CHECKING ID", "pair account b": "CARD ID", "window days": 5}' The answer's links is how many historical pairs such a rule would link, and sample shows a few of them with their dates and gap days.

sections.heading: Activating a pair rule
sections.text: Because the nightly sweep looks at all of your posted history, activating one of these applies it retroactively. Purser therefore tells you how many historical pairs it would link — with the rule's own window — and asks you to confirm that number: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/$RULE ID/state \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"state": "active", "confirm links": 12}' The count is computed by the same selection the sweep then runs, so it is the number that links: pairs of one-sided rows merged into a transfer, and rows absorbed into an existing transfer that was waiting for its other side. It matches what the preview above reported for the same history. The confirmation is not ceremony. Merging two rows is balance-neutral, so the post-sync balance check that catches most mistakes cannot see a wrong one — every balance stays correct while two unrelated rows are silently one. The count is your check instead. Use effective from to bound it, or narrow window days, if the number looks high. An active pair rule cannot be edited in a way that changes what it links (the pair, amount exact, effective from, window days or its payee scope): the edit is refused. Disable the rule, edit it, and activate it again, so a wider scope goes through the same confirmation. The Rules page reads each rule as words with account and category names — for example Payee contains "acme" on Checking , then Category Fitness — and keeps the stored one-line form, with paths, under As stored for matching a rule against an audit row. The Applied column on the Rules page (applied count on GET /rules, applied in the MCP list rules tool) counts how many times a rule has fired. A pair rule counts each link it makes, merged pairs and absorbed rows alike, including the links the nightly sweep makes after you activate it. A categorize or rename rule counts each new row it shapes, and a run over history counts once. Previews and the confirmation count above never add to it, and unlinking a transfer does not take a count back.

sections.heading: Applying a rule to history
sections.text: New rules do not quietly rewrite the past. POST /rules/{id}/apply-history is the only path, and it is a dry run unless you say otherwise: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/$RULE ID/apply-history \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"dry run": true}' The dry run's counts are the real run's results — both walk the same candidate list. That list covers all of your history, however long: the preview samples the newest 5,000 rows (scan capped says when it stopped there), but apply-history examines every live row and reports how many as scanned. By default it touches uncategorized rows and rows automation categorized, and leaves anything you categorized alone; overriding your own choices is opt-in. Posted rows are skipped unless you ask for posted: "correct", which mints a proper reversal and replacement for each one. A categorize rule never touches a transfer, which has no category to set — not even with include user categorized. Transfers its predicate matches are left out of matched and reported as skipped transfers. Rows in a different currency from the rule's category are left out the same way and reported as skipped currency: a transaction keeps one currency. Split transactions (one bank amount across several categories, from a QIF import) are read-only and left out the same way, reported as skipped splits. A rule whose category is an [account] leaves out a row whose only counterpart in that account is the other side of a pair you said is not a transfer, reported as skipped not a transfer. That is the one count where the real run can differ from its dry run: when an earlier row of the same run takes the counterpart a later row would have paired with, the later row is skipped as it is applied and counted there instead. transfer link rules have no apply-history: the nightly sweep is their retroactive application.

sections.heading: From an agent
sections.text: Three MCP tools mirror this: list rules shows the active set in evaluation order, preview rule dry-runs a predicate, and propose rule creates one: a draft, or an active rule with activate=true when you asked the agent for it. There is no MCP tool to activate a draft later; that happens on the Rules page or over REST. For a pair, pass pair accounts (two account paths) to preview rule and propose rule, with an optional window days. The preview's links is the count the activation will ask you to confirm, and list rules shows each pair rule's window days and, for a payee-scoped one, its payee scope. An agent may also accept a transfer-link suggestion with decide suggestion: that creates the rule as a draft; activating it confirms its projected link count, on the Rules page or over REST.

sections.text: - Manage transfers — the bracket sugar and manual linking - Categories — why a category is an account - Suggestions inbox — where a confirm's proposed pair rule waits - DESIGN.md sections 5 (matching), 7.1 (import order) and 11 (optional AI), plus decisions 46, 66 and 67

pages.title: Scheduled transactions and recurring bills
pages.description: Create schedules, let Purser materialize and match expected instances, and surface late bills and price changes.

sections.text: A scheduled transaction (a schedule in the API and MCP tools) is a recurring expectation — the $60.00 gym membership on the 1st, the paycheck every other Friday. Purser materializes each schedule into expected transactions, matches them against what actually clears, and tells you when a bill is late or its price changed.

sections.heading: Create a schedule
sections.text: Recurrence is an RFC 5545 RRULE (the same syntax calendars use). Create a schedule on the admin UI's Scheduled transactions page (its cadence picker writes the rule for you), over REST (POST /schedules) or MCP with create schedule — an agent that parses a statement email calls this tool directly (Purser never parses email server-side). The schedule is created active. An agent acting on its own initiative passes propose=true instead, and the schedule lands as a suggestion that your decision turns into the schedule (decide suggestion). A proposal can carry a note (up to 200 characters, such as the statement line the agent read) for whoever decides it, and is refused when the account already has a schedule for that payee or counterparty. { "payee": "Acme Gym", "memo": "Family membership", "account": "assets.checking", "rrule": "FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1", "dtstart": "2026-09-01", "amount": "-60.00", "category": "expenses.personal.fitness" } A schedule has a payee (who you pay or who pays you) and an optional memo . A flat schedule needs a payee unless it has a memo; a transfer needs neither, since the other account says who it is with. The schedule's name is derived, not entered: the memo, else the payee, else the transfer's other account. It is the description its expected transactions carry. Editing the payee or memo relabels the live instances whose label you have not changed yourself; send "" to clear either one. Clients written before payee and memo existed may still send name: without a memo it becomes a transfer's memo, a flat schedule's payee when no payee is sent, and otherwise its memo. Amounts are decimal strings; negative is money out. amount type defaults to fixed for a bill that is the same every period; estimated schedules take their amount from confirmed matches (estimate basis: last, rolling avg 3, rolling avg 12) with amount as the fallback before any history exists. Once two settled amounts differ, the forecast shows an estimated occurrence with its range — the lowest and highest of the last six together with the estimate (see Estimate range). dtstart is the rule's anchor — the date the recurrence counts from. Rules that name their day (BYMONTHDAY=6,20, BYDAY=FR) barely need it; rules that do not (FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2 — every other week) take their phase from it, so pass the last real occurrence. FREQ must be DAILY or coarser.

sections.heading: Recurring transfers
sections.text: A card payment, a loan payment, a 529 or IRA contribution is a transfer between two of your accounts, not a bill against a category. Give the schedule a counterparty account instead of a category: { "name": "Citi card payment", "account": "assets.checking", "counterparty account": "liabilities.citicard", "rrule": "FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=5", "dtstart": "2026-09-05", "amount type": "estimated", "estimate basis": "counterparty balance" } Its instances are two-leg expected transfers — the schedule account's leg is amount (negative = money leaves it), the counterparty's leg the opposite — so they show up in both accounts' forecasts, and when the bank rows on both sides arrive and link into one transfer, the matcher settles the expectation against that merged row (no double count). The schedule is itself what links those rows when their descriptors say nothing about a transfer, and the two sides may post on different days — see Scheduled transfers. The counterparty balance basis sizes each instance from the counterparty's reported balance: "pay the card in full". For a card that is the current balance, charges since the statement closed included, so record the statement when it arrives (next section). The whats new week of upcoming bills reads an instance from the schedule account's leg, the side that pays: a card or loan payment due this week is listed with its (negative) amount and counts toward the total, while a transfer into the schedule's account (a sweep from savings, say) is money arriving, not a bill.

sections.heading: Card statement balances
sections.text: A card payment estimated from the card's current balance usually runs high: you pay the statement balance from the last close, and the card has new charges since. Purser cannot read statements (SimpleFIN carries no statement figure), so you or your agent record it against the payment it is due on — on the Scheduled transactions page ( Statement on a card payment's instance), over REST, or with MCP record statement balance. An agent reading a statement email ("statement balance 8,347.00, payment due October 19") makes one call: { "account": "liabilities.citicard", "statement balance": "8347.00", "due date": "2026-10-19", "statement date": "2026-09-22" } statement balance is the figure as printed: the amount owed, positive. Purser finds the card's live payment instance due nearest due date (within 14 days), sets it to the statement balance on both legs (-8347.00 from checking), and pins it, so the current-balance estimate no longer moves it; the next cycle's payment keeps following the balance. Over REST (POST /schedules/statement-balance) you can name the instance by transaction id instead of account and due date. The statement, its closing date and who recorded it stay on the instance, the instance and the forecast report basis: statement, and recording again replaces the figure. Reset the instance to go back to the current balance. Recording needs write scope and works on credit card payments only; a loan payment, or any other bill, is an ordinary override (below). Paying the exact statement amount also lets the schedule link the payment's bank rows (it vouches only for its exact amount).

sections.heading: Rules and instances
sections.text: The schedule is the durable rule . What you actually see in a register and in the forecast are its instances : expected transactions materialized on a rolling 60-day horizon, nightly and whenever a schedule is activated or edited. Each instance fills one slot of the rule (its occurrence date), and materialization never creates a second instance for a slot that already has one — matched, skipped, or edited. Instances are yours to edit; the rule never overrides what you touched: - Override an occurrence — a different amount ("this month's card payment is 8,067.37") or date ("it lands on the 3rd") — with the ordinary transaction edit (PATCH /transactions/{id}, MCP override instance). The instance becomes pinned : estimate refreshes and rule edits leave it alone. On a transfer schedule both legs move: the amount is the schedule account's leg in the schedule's sign (-8067.37 for a card payment from checking), or the leg of the account a PATCH names in account ({"amount": "8067.37", "account": "liabilities.citicard"} from the card's side). An amount whose sign would reverse the transfer is refused. A card's statement balance has its own path, which keeps the statement on the instance (see Card statement balances). - Relabel an occurrence — a different description or payee. A label is not an override: the instance stays un-pinned and keeps following the estimate. - Reset an overridden occurrence (POST /transactions/{id}/reset-instance, MCP reset instance, write scope; the Reset button on a pinned row in the Scheduled transactions page). The pin is cleared and the instance takes the rule's date (its slot), name, payee and current estimate again, and a recorded card statement is removed. If the rule no longer has that slot, or estimates nothing, the instance is dropped instead. - Skip an occurrence (POST /transactions/{id}/void, MCP skip instance). The slot stays filled, so the occurrence does not come back. - Mark paid by matching the instance to a posted row (POST /matching/match, MCP match). When the matcher already proposed that very pair, this confirms the proposal — the unmatched report (GET /matching/unmatched, MCP list unmatched) names the proposed bank row as proposed posted id — and a row proposed for a different bill is refused, with the error naming that bill. The rule side: an estimated schedule refreshes its live, un-pinned instances whenever a new confirmed match moves the estimate (audited as schedule.refresh). Editing the rule (PATCH /schedules/{id}, MCP update schedule) resyncs: slots the new rule no longer produces are voided and released, survivors are re-estimated, missing slots materialize — and editing back re-fills the released slots. Renaming a schedule (or changing its payee) relabels its live instances, pinned ones too: every instance whose description is still the old name takes the new one, and so does a payee that is still the old one — a schedule without a payee uses its name as its instances' payee. A description or payee you set yourself is kept. Pause stops expecting (live un-pinned instances are dropped and come back on resume ); end is terminal and keeps history (POST /schedules/{id}/pause, /resume, /end; MCP end schedule with action set to pause, resume or end). GET /schedules/{id} lists the live instances with their slot, pinned and overdue flags; next due is always the earliest live instance — an overdue one counts, because it is still due. In the admin UI the same actions live on the Scheduled transactions page (expand a schedule for its instances; pinned rows carry Reset) and on the account register, where a materialized row carries a scheduled badge with Override, Mark paid and Skip.

sections.heading: Expected instances and matching
sections.text: The matcher reconciles each instance against the real posted or pending row when it arrives. The posted amount always wins — the expectation is replaced by reality, and the difference is recorded as a variance. Variance feeds future estimates, and a breach beyond the threshold emits a variance.threshold event. A match to a pending row follows that row. When the bank posts it, the match moves to the posted row and the bill stays paid (a proposed match is decided again against the posted row). If the bank drops the pending instead, the match is released and the instance comes back as expected, in the same slot and with any override you made, so it can go late or match the charge the bank really posts. Voiding the pending yourself (POST /transactions/{id}/void) does the same: a confirmed match is released the same way, and a proposed match is withdrawn so the bill can be matched again. While a match is only proposed , the bank row is already in the balance, so the forecast and the whats new week of upcoming bills treat the instance as paid, pending your confirmation, and the forecast's coverage counts it in matches pending. Estimates only learn from posted amounts: a pending amount can still change, so it moves the estimate (and raises a recurring.price changed event) only once the posted row lands — whether the bank posts it, you post the pending yourself (POST /transactions/{id}/post), or the bank's posted row for the other side of a pending transfer arrives and posts the whole transfer.

sections.heading: Late bills
sections.text: When an expected instance passes its window unmatched, Purser emits a bill.late event. Late bills surface three ways: the event stream (and any webhook), the whats new MCP digest, and the Dashboard's Needs attention card, which collects late bills alongside the suggestions awaiting your decision. A late bill the matcher has proposed a bank row for shows as that proposal's match card instead: accept it to mark the bill paid, or reject it so that row is never proposed for the bill again.

sections.heading: Low-balance warnings
sections.text: To be warned before an account runs low, give it a floor: in the app, Set floor in the account's register header; over REST, PATCH /accounts/{id} with {"min balance": "500.00"}; or have your agent call update account(account, min balance="500.00"). Each night Purser projects the next 30 days of every account with a floor, schedules included, and emits a forecast.shortfall event when the projection drops below it. Clear the floor (null, or "" in update account) to stop the warnings. See Shortfalls for the sign rules and which account types take a floor.

sections.heading: Detected schedules
sections.text: Purser also proposes schedules it finds for you. Every night (and on POST /schedules/detect / MCP detect schedules) it scans your history per account and counterparty — a payee for ordinary bills, the other account for transfers such as card payments, loan payments and contributions — and each recurring pattern becomes a suggestion in the suggestions inbox with the evidence attached: the occurrences, the cadence it found (weekly, every two or four weeks, semi-monthly, monthly, every two/three/six months, yearly), how regular the gaps were, and how steady the amount was. A varying amount is not a veto — card payments that swing threefold are still monthly; they come through as estimated (paying the card's balance when the counterparty is a card). A single skipped month is tolerated; a pattern that stopped is not proposed. Lapsed detector cards are hidden and withdrawn on the next scan. A changed latest amount after a stable history is shown explicitly for verification; opposite-sign histories do not form a single schedule. See the safeguards for the evidence rules. Adding a credit card or loan account triggers the same scan for payments to it right away (source = account added). Detected patterns never auto-activate — accepting the suggestion is the only path to an active schedule, and rejecting one is remembered.

sections.heading: Price changes
sections.text: list recurring is the subscription radar: every active outflow schedule with an honest monthly-equivalent total (annual and semi-annual bills normalized), its next due date, and its last price change, all computed server-side — never sum the rows yourself. A schedule you accepted from a suggestion is as active as one you created: its source (manual, detected or agent) only records where it came from. Patterns still waiting for your decision are not listed; suggestions open counts them, and they live in the suggestions inbox. In MCP Apps hosts the recurring widget shows that count as a footer. When a recurring charge posts at a new amount, Purser emits a recurring.price changed event and the change lands in that price history, so "what am I paying, and what changed?" is one tool call. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md sections 6 (schedules and forecasting) and 5 (matching). See the MCP tool catalog for list recurring, create schedule, update schedule, end schedule, skip instance, override instance, reset instance and record statement balance. Recurrence detection counts each correction chain once, using its latest replacement. Editing a posted bank transaction does not double its amount in the history, whether the correction was made by a person, an agent or a rule.

sections.heading: Estimate certainty on one occurrence
sections.text: An Estimate badge identifies an uncertain amount, date, or both. Open its accessible details in Scheduled transactions or the forecast to see the basis, evidence and original estimate. Confirmed upcoming is still scheduled; it is not posted cash. Match awaiting review is a proposal, while Matched actual identifies a linked posted transaction. A link to a pending bank entry is labelled separately. A schedule's date type is fixed or estimated (MCP date mode). Use an estimated date for an approved reimbursement with an uncertain deposit date, or a seasonal service whose arrival varies. Historical detection remains an inference even when the previous amounts were identical. Use Update evidence on an occurrence to change one dimension. The REST operation is PATCH /schedules/instances/{transaction id}/certainty; the MCP tool is update occurrence certainty. For example, a paystub can confirm this paycheck's amount without changing the date or confirming next month's pay: { "amount": { "state": "confirmed", "value": "2150.00", "source": "payroll", "as of": "2026-11-15", "note": "Net amount on this occurrence's paystub" } } Omit value to keep the current amount or date. Omit the other dimension entirely to leave it alone. Every change needs a source, as-of date and evidence note. history can support an estimate but cannot confirm an obligation. Confirmation never creates a posted transaction. A generic amount/date override is not confirmation evidence, and only changes that dimension's certainty. Confirmed dimensions survive automatic estimate refresh. Reset returns the occurrence to its rule but retains the original and superseded evidence. The original snapshot stays available after edits, refreshes, matching and unmatching; older occurrences migrated into this feature are labelled First retained snapshot , because their earlier estimates were not recorded. Read full details with GET /schedules/instances/{transaction id}/certainty or MCP get schedule occurrence. Schedule detail also returns its most recent 50 matched occurrences. Actual amount and timing differences are computed against the original; positive timing variance means later. For a card payment, recording a statement confirms only its amount. Unmatching preserves that evidence; reset explicitly hands it back to the rule. An estimate or an ambiguous candidate never resolves automatically. Accept or reject its match proposal, or explicitly match the occurrence to the correct posted transaction. The posted movement replaces its forecast contribution, so it is counted once. Pending-review proposals retain the existing per-account forecast treatment; rejecting them restores the expected contribution.

sections.heading: Evidence on projected slots
sections.text: A fixed amount is a calculation choice, not proof that a future payment is known. Keep amount type="fixed" when the model should use the entered Decimal amount. Changing it to estimated selects a history-based estimator and can change the forecast. To mark a fixed planning value uncertain without changing it, annotate its occurrence instead. For a projection beyond the 60-day materialization window, use the forecast Upcoming occurrences and estimate details list and Update evidence . The amount calculation is shown separately from the Estimate label. This form keeps the amount and date unchanged. REST: GET or PATCH /schedules/{schedule id}/occurrences/{occurrence date}/certainty. MCP: pass schedule id and occurrence date to get schedule occurrence or update occurrence certainty, instead of transaction id. Forecast detail includes that address in certainty.slot. For example: { "schedule id": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001", "occurrence date": "2027-02-01", "amount": { "state": "estimated", "source": "agent", "as of": "2026-11-15", "note": "Fixed planning value; no statement for this occurrence yet" } } Omit value. A slot address rejects a different amount or date even after the slot materializes; use the existing transaction endpoint for an intentional value edit. Annotate the date separately when its timing is approximate. One slot's confirmation never confirms the following slot. Unannotated fixed rules retain their existing certainty defaults; annotate each relevant slot explicitly. The first annotation saves a First retained snapshot with its real capture time. Evidence, attribution and history follow the slot into materialization and rematerialization. If a rule changes the calculated value, the earlier evidence stays visible, with its previous value, and the current value is estimated. {"clear": ["amount"]} returns amount certainty to its rule default without changing the amount; superseded evidence remains in the REST detail's history. For existing plans, first record the forecast's amounts, dates and daily balances, then apply evidence with no value fields. Re-read the forecast to verify that only certainty changed. The schema migration does not annotate existing plans, recalculate history, extend the materialization horizon, or create transactions.

pages.title: Connect banks with SimpleFIN
pages.description: Claim a SimpleFIN setup token, map feed accounts to the ledger, schedule syncs, backfill history, and scope each account with feed_start.

sections.text: SimpleFIN Bridge is Purser's live feed path: an aggregator hands the Bridge your bank data, and Purser fetches it on a schedule. Every payload is archived verbatim to the append-only raw fetches archive before anything touches the ledger, and every imported row traces back to those bytes. A row's identity is its content — account, date, amount and description — never the bank's transaction id, which can change between fetches. Two identical charges on one day (the same merchant, the same amount) are still two rows: within one fetch, the second identical row is the second occurrence of that content, an identity of its own. Every sync re-fetches the last seven days so pending charges can settle, and that overlap adds nothing, because each fetch numbers its identical rows from one again and lands on identities already in the ledger.

sections.heading: Connect
sections.text: Get a setup token from your SimpleFIN Bridge account page and paste it into the first-run wizard, or later into Settings - Connections . Setup tokens are one-time secrets — paste them only into Purser, never into a chat. Purser exchanges the token once for an encrypted access URL (stored encrypted at rest; it never appears in logs) and discovers the accounts the connection exposes.

sections.heading: Map feed accounts to ledger accounts
sections.text: Discovered feed accounts are not ledger accounts until you map them. The setup wizard's map step covers the accounts found at setup; an account your bank adds later shows as not in Purser yet , first under its bank, in Settings - Connections . Select Map beside it (admins only) and either create a new Purser account (name, type and ledger path; cards and loans default under liabilities.) or pick an existing open account in the same currency. Picking an account that another feed account already feeds moves the feed onto the new one. The already-fetched transactions import as soon as you map. Only mapped accounts sync. Closing a ledger account unmaps it, and the feed account reappears as unmapped — reopen and remap to resume. Until you decide, the Dashboard lists each such account under bank accounts not in Purser yet , with a link that opens its row.

sections.heading: Ignore an account you do not want
sections.text: Select Ignore instead of Map when the account should stay out of the ledger. The usual case is a joint account that two bank logins can both see: SimpleFIN delivers it once per login, and only one copy should be mapped. The page says so when an unmapped account has the name of a mapped one. An ignored account is listed last with Track again , is no longer reported as waiting (in the app, or to agents as not connected), and nothing about it is imported or deleted. Mapping it later imports its fetched transactions as usual. For checking, savings, cash and card accounts, discovery also shows the bank's available balance when it differs from the balance: the cash you can spend, or the credit left on a card. Each discovered account names its bank login: org is the login's name and conn id its SimpleFIN id. Two logins at one bank (for example, two people who share a joint account) show as two logins, each listing its own copy of the shared account; map one of them. If two accounts in one fetch arrive with the same id, both are flagged ambiguous and neither syncs until the bank sends distinct ids.

sections.heading: Read bank balances without administration
sections.text: GET /accounts/{id}, GET /accounts/{id}/balance and MCP account balance include the same bank snapshot with ordinary read scope. No connection discovery or administrator identity is needed. The account detail and balance surfaces include it; account lists stay compact. Reading it does not sync the feed, record a reconciliation, learn a new basis or change financial data. Normal read auditing still applies. - kind: latest means the most recent archived sync report, even if the enclosing ledger balance was requested with a historical as of date. - balance is the bank-reported balance; available balance is separate and retained even when equal to it. Available balance can mean remaining credit on a card, and is neither ledger cash nor simply balance minus pending items. available balance status distinguishes reported, missing and invalid values. - Amounts are decimal strings in currency. Missing or invalid amounts are null, never zero. source identifies SimpleFIN without revealing bank numbers, external identifiers, credential URLs or other accounts in the payload. - balance at preserves a real source instant (epochs rendered in UTC; an ISO timestamp retains its offset). This does not identify the bank's local time zone. balance date is the UTC date of an instant, or the original date-only value. time precision is timestamp, date or unknown; date-only values never acquire a midnight timestamp. fetched at is the separate ingestion timestamp, not the time the bank measured its balance. - freshness is fresh, stale, future or unknown. age days compares balance date with the ledger day; staleness uses feed stale days. - status distinguishes disconnected/closed/disabled accounts, no snapshot, an account missing from the payload, ambiguous provider IDs and missing or invalid bank balances. Unknown values and comparisons stay null. For eligible cash/card accounts (and opted-in manual brokerage cash), comparison includes live posted-only and pending-inclusive totals, the selected ledger balance, effective basis, basis learned, basis pinned and exact difference = bank balance - selected ledger balance. ledger cutoff: all recorded dates explicitly includes future-dated live postings. It is not a historical reconstruction at the bank timestamp. Unavailable comparisons have a comparison unavailable reason, including unknown/mismatched currency or an ineligible account type. matches either basis is separate from the exact difference: the existing drift-warning policy considers the account clean if either ledger basis matches. For example, a bank balance of "100.00", posted balance of "100.0000" and pending-inclusive balance of "85.0000" give a difference of "15.0000" when pending-inclusive is pinned, but matches either basis is true. Reading the snapshot does not change that alert policy or its gates.

sections.heading: Bank errors and connection status
sections.text: Purser asks SimpleFIN for protocol version 2, which tags every error with a code and, where it applies, the bank login or account it concerns: Code Meaning What to do --- --- --- con.auth A bank login needs attention Log in to that bank again in SimpleFIN Bridge act.failed, act.missingdata One account's data could not be fetched completely Usually clears on a later sync gen.auth SimpleFIN rejected Purser's access Reconnect with a new setup token gen.api A note for developers, such as a request window longer than the Bridge recommends Nothing A sync whose fetch carries a con. or act. error, or gen.auth, sets the connection's status to warning; the next clean fetch sets it back to active. GET /connections lists the latest fetch's errors as last issues (code, message, conn id, account id) beside the plain messages in last errors, and a sync result carries the same issues. A server that still answers in version 1 sends messages without codes; they read as code gen., and any of them sets warning.

sections.heading: Know when a bank stops updating
sections.text: A bank can stop updating while every sync still succeeds: SimpleFIN keeps returning the last balance it saw. After each sync Purser checks every bank login and every mapped account and raises an event when a problem starts and again when it clears: - feed.auth required — a bank login needs you to log in again; - feed.account failed — an account failed to download on two syncs in a row; - feed.stale — an account's bank balance date is more than feed stale days old (default 4; set it with PUT /config or PURSER FEED STALE DAYS); - feed.recovered — one of these cleared. The agent digest (whats new) lists what is open in its feed section on every call until it is fixed, so a daily brief keeps naming the bank. When a bank needs a new login, log in again in SimpleFIN Bridge; the next sync clears the problem.

sections.heading: Recover what a bank outage missed
sections.text: While a bank is stuck, every sync still succeeds, so each sync asks only for the last few days. When the bank comes back it has the outage's transactions, older than that window. Purser notices the account's balance date jump past the window and, in the same sync, fetches that account again from the date it froze (focused requests of at most 45 days each, reaching at most 90 days back, the Bridge's limit). The sync result and audit row report it as gap repair. If the day's fetch budget is spent or the request fails, the repair is kept and the next sync runs it. When the outage began more than 90 days ago, gap repair.unreachable before marks the date before which rows must be imported by hand (QIF or CSV). For a gap the automatic repair did not see (for example one from before this feature), re-fetch a range yourself: curl -X POST "$PURSER URL/connections/$CONNECTION ID/refetch" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"start": "2026-08-10", "end": "2026-10-12", "accounts": ["assets.checking"]}' end defaults to today and may be at most 90 days after start (fetched in 45-day pages, each one of the day's 24 fetches); accounts are ledger paths and default to every mapped account. Agents use the MCP tool refetch feed. Rows already in the ledger are skipped, so a repeat run imports nothing.

sections.heading: Bank health in the app
sections.text: Settings - Connections shows the same picture for people. Each connection opens with a summary in words (how many banks need a new login, how many accounts are not in Purser yet or have stopped updating), then one list of every bank login with its status (ok, needs login, error) and each account it delivers with the Purser account it feeds (or "not in Purser yet"), its bank balance date and age (stale ones flagged), and what the latest sync carried. Re-fetch a date range runs the refetch described above for a range and the accounts you pick. Stale after (days) next to the sync schedule sets feed stale days. After Sync now , a note says what an outage repair recovered or why it was postponed.
